## 1. Vehicle routing problem

### Constraints and criteria

Constraints turn a single traveling salesman problem (TSP) tour into several routes, the routes of a vehicle routing problem (VRP). When a potential route violates a constraint, e.g., a limit on total route distance, total route time, vehicle capacity, or delivery/pickup time windows, its cost can be set to infinity so that it is never selected.

The TSP of Lecture 5.1 can be thought of as the unconstrained routing problem. With no constraint, a tour such as Lecture 5.1’s through the 100 counties of North Carolina returns to its starting point wherever it starts, like a pilgrimage, and it does not matter how long it takes. In practice, once constraints are put on, a route can no longer travel any distance it likes. Each route may be limited by its distance, which would be one constraint, but more realistically by its total time. Truck drivers, by law or just in practice, do not want to be on the road more than about eight hours if they can help it: they want to be back home every day, and a carrier that can offer routes that leave and return to where they started within eight hours keeps more loyal drivers in a trade with a lot of turnover. One way to keep a driver’s day that short on a long haul is a truck relay. In a relay, a driver takes a trailer only part of the way to its destination and drops it off at a meeting point, which needs to be little more than a parking lot, where another driver hooks it up and takes it on, so that each driver drives one leg and can return home the same day. A small company being set up at the Port of Wilmington, for example, was looking at a relay for product delivered to the port and going on further south. Its drivers would take the trailers from Wilmington as far as Augusta, Georgia, park them there, and be back in Wilmington within an eight-hour day, while drivers coming from Savannah, Atlanta and points south would hook up the trailers and take them on to their destinations. Without the relay, one driver going from Wilmington to Atlanta would need at least an overnight stay, which attracts fewer people to the job. By law a driver can drive up to 11 hours, and with loading and unloading time that makes a day of 13 or 14 hours, so time is an important constraint. Vehicles are also physically limited in capacity when product is actually delivered. The TSP alone is appropriate when no cargo is carried, as in visiting every county seat in North Carolina, where any notion of capacity is irrelevant, but a vehicle with a finite capacity in weight and cube adds another constraint. The final constraint seen quite often is a delivery or pickup time window: a route cannot be planned to arrive whenever, but must arrive within a fairly tight window. Windows matter less in the United States, where land is cheap and a distribution center can have a dedicated loading dock for each store it serves. Europe has always been very constrained in space and has long had very tight delivery windows, and near a distribution center trucks can be seen parked beside the road, next to a field, having arrived early because of uncertainty and waiting an hour or two for a window of perhaps an hour, since there is no space to wait at the distribution center itself. There, time windows are a very important constraint.

The VRP is the TSP with vehicle constraints added. The constraints can be some combination of the following: capacity (weight, cube, etc.); maximum TC (hours of service, HOS: 11 hr max); time windows (with/without delay at customer), where the VRP uses absolute windows that can be checked by simple scanning, while project scheduling uses relative windows solved by shortest path with negative arcs, as in Lecture 4.1; and the maximum number of routes/vehicles, which is hard to enforce. Its criteria are the number of routes/vehicles and the TC (time or distance). A VRP solution can be one time or periodic: a one time (operational) VRP minimizes TC, and a periodic (tactical) VRP minimizes TLC, a route sometimes called a “milk run,” the case of Lecture 5.2.

The VRP is best thought of as the TSP plus additional vehicle constraints, or the TSP as the unconstrained version of the VRP. From a technical point of view the TSP is easy, since any permutation is a feasible tour; because of its additional vehicle constraints, the likelihood that a random permutation is feasible for a VRP approaches zero. So with the VRP most of the work is in constructing a feasible solution, whereas with the TSP most of the work is taking any solution and improving it, the easy and hard construction of Lecture 5.1, Sec. 3. For the TSP, 2-opt does most of the heavy lifting, and the improvement over a random start can be very large; for the VRP, the construction procedure typically gets most of the way, and improvement afterward usually adds no more than about 5%. The two are related problems of different types. The most common constraints are capacity, in weight, in cube or in both, the physical capacity of a truck, and a maximum total cost: with the cost of a route taken as its travel time, the hours of service of Lecture 3.2 can be modeled, under which a driver who has reached the driving limit cannot drive again until enough time off has passed, and drivers are very conscious of reaching it. Time windows are another type of constraint, and they differ from capacity and maximum distance or time, which are geographic: on a map of routes, if the routes do not cross each other, they are probably good with respect to capacity and maximum distance or time, but a time window cannot be seen in the sequence of a route’s stops, since time is not a dimension of the map. With windows, two routes may overlap in a way that would be poor geographically for minimizing distance and still make sense. Windows can be with or without delay at a customer. With a window opening at 3:00, before which the loading dock cannot be reached and within which the load is dropped off by 4:00, a truck arriving at 2:30 either waits 30 minutes, which is feasible with delay, or is infeasible, since without delay it must arrive at 3:00 exactly. No delay can have a physical reason, there being no place for the truck to wait, but it can also be computational: even when the vehicle could wait, enforcing no delay can give better solutions, since it eliminates the possibilities that arrive early and forces a harder look for ones that arrive right at the start of a window. In practice, because of the uncertainty in driving, no window can be hit exactly, and a route planned to arrive at 3:00 would aim to arrive at least 10 or 15 minutes early.

The one constraint that cannot be handled by setting the cost of a violation to infinity is a maximum number of routes. With a limit of four routes, the savings procedure of Lecture 5.2 may create five or six, each feasible with respect to every constraint except the limit on vehicles, because savings starts with a dedicated route for each shipment, 100 routes for 100 shipments, and narrows them down to the number needed to minimize cost; a maximum number of routes would take extra work to incorporate. As for the criteria, what dominates everything else is the number of vehicles: most companies would rather have routes that need four vehicles and a total of 1,000 miles than five vehicles and 800 or 900 miles, since an extra hour of driving is marginal, while another vehicle means another driver. Minimizing distance or time is the secondary criterion, and minimizing the number of vehicles the primary one. Routes and vehicles are not always the same: when routes are time based, as with time windows, one truck can run several of them, a morning route that ends by noon and then an afternoon route, so the number of vehicles is sometimes less than the number of routes, the subject of Sec. 3.

Another objective is minimizing the number of routes. It is not exactly the same as minimizing the number of vehicles, but in between that and the traditional objective, minimizing the total cost of all of the routes. Especially when trying to reduce the number of vehicles, it may be better to increase the number of routes, shorter routes that one vehicle can run one after another without overlap. Also, a problem can have a fixed number of vehicles, and then a set of routes is fine as long as it does not need more vehicles than that.

Most vehicle routing research gives little attention to minimizing the number of vehicles, which, given the many thousands of papers published, is a real gap in what is done in vehicle routing. One possible tool is the ability to estimate route distances: if every vehicle can carry, say, 20 packages and the number of stops is known, the distances can be estimated, and an estimate that at least six vehicles are needed allows a start with six vehicles, trying to reach as many customers as possible at minimum distance with them. The focus is then not on minimizing the number of vehicles, but on first calculating the number to use and then doing the best with those, a different way of approaching routing problems from the procedures of Lecture 5.2, and the subject of Sec. 4. The VRP itself can be a one-time operational problem, a single set of routes, or, just as with estimating the TSP in Lecture 5.1, a tactical problem in which the routes are run on a regular basis, a series of deliveries made to the same customers every week. Such a route is called a milk run: a vehicle might come to a supplier twice a week, say, to pick up product and carry it to a manufacturing facility. It works because the production process is fairly constant, so a standardized set of routes repeated on a regular basis makes sense. To find the best set of milk runs, the total logistics cost has to be considered, both inventory and transport cost, whereas the operational problem looks only at the distance or travel time, because the size of each load has already been determined. This is the routing version of what Lectures 3.2 and 3.3 did for freight transport, first one-time point-to-point shipments and then the periodic case, and the periodic version minimizes total logistics cost in the same way.

### Routing from a depot

The VRP from a depot is stated as a model in Model 1. It is the TSP of Model 1 in Lecture 5.1 with its tour divided into routes, each beginning and ending at the depot and each feasible: within the vehicle’s capacity, and within any other constraint a single route must satisfy. What changes from Lecture 5.1’s model is marked. Its objective is the cost of the routes alone, not first the number of vehicles, as in the operational VRP of Model 3 in Lecture 1.1; the reason is taken up with Model 3, in Sec. 3.

minimize: total cost of ~~a tour through every node~~ the routes

solve for:
(a) ~~tour, a sequence that visits each node exactly once and returns to its starting node~~ routes, each a sequence of customers that begins and ends at the depot.

subject to:
(a) Leave: each ~~node~~ customer is left exactly once;
(b) Enter: each ~~node~~ customer is entered exactly once;
(c) ~~Single tour: the arcs used form one connected cycle through all the nodes, not several~~ Routes: the arcs used form cycles, each passing through the depot;
(d) Feasible routes: each route satisfies every constraint on a single route, such as the vehicle’s capacity, a maximum distance or time, or time windows.

assumptions:
(a) arc costs are given and need not be symmetric;
(b) cost of a ~~tour~~ route is ~~the sum of the costs of its arcs, including the return to the start~~ given by a route cost, the route’s distance or time when it is feasible and infinity when it is not.

Model 1: Vehicle routing from a depot

Generalization of Model 1: Traveling salesman problem in Lecture 5.1

The procedures of Lecture 5.2 solve a VRP with no change. Suppose a route being created is feasible with respect to whatever constraints there are, and one more shipment is considered for it. If adding that shipment would violate one of the constraints, the cost of the route, which would otherwise be its time or its distance, is simply set to infinity. When the pairwise savings procedure then tries to combine routes, the infinite cost of the combined route makes its saving negative infinity, and since the savings procedure considers only positive savings, every pair whose combination is infeasible is eliminated at once. The savings procedure uses the minimum cost insertion procedure, and the same holds there: when it tries an insertion that makes a route infeasible, the cost of that route comes back as infinity, and the insertion is never chosen. It is a simple way to account for constraints.

With a single capacity, as in Ex. 1, the route cost of Model 1 is a route’s total cost when the demand on it is within the capacity and infinity otherwise, so that no procedure minimizing cost ever selects it:

$$
c(r) = \begin{cases}
TC(r), & \text{if } \displaystyle\sum_{i \in r} q_i \le K \\[6pt]
\infty, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
$$

where

- $r$ = route, a sequence of customers from the depot back to it
- $TC(r)$ = total cost of route $r$, its distance or its time
- $q_i$ = demand of customer $i$, in the units of the capacity
- $K$ = capacity of the vehicle, in any unit: tons, cubic feet, cases or seats.

The formulation of Model 1 is then the savings procedure of Lecture 5.2, with the route cost as its $c(R)$, whatever constraints the route cost holds:

Model 1 formulation: Savings

```text
algorithm savings;
{ input:  shipments 1, …, n; cost c(R), ∞ for an infeasible route }
{ output: routes, each shipment on exactly one                    }
begin
    Rₖ := (k, k) for each shipment k;
    sᵢⱼ := c(Rᵢ) + c(Rⱼ) − c(best route of i and j), each pair i < j;
    list the pairs with sᵢⱼ > 0 in decreasing order of sᵢⱼ;
    for each pair (i, j) in the list do
        if i and j are on different routes then
        begin
            S, T := the shorter and the longer of their two routes;
            R′ := T;
            for each shipment k on S do R′ := mincostinsert(k, R′);
            if c(R′) < ∞ then T := R′, S := ∅;   { the merge kept }
        end;
    return the routes that are not empty;
end;
```

Logjam exports it, as in Lecture 5.2, and Ex. 1(c) runs it with this route cost:

A constraint special to a particular problem is added by defining a route total cost function of its own. Its first input is the route, followed by whatever other information the constraint needs, such as a maximum distance. It does not reinvent the wheel: it calls the route total cost function already in use, with whatever constraints that function already incorporates, to get the route’s total cost, and then a single if statement sets the total cost to infinity when it exceeds the maximum distance. Any constraint could replace the maximum distance: if there were a way of identifying a left turn, the cost of any route involving one could be set to infinity. This gives a great deal of flexibility to incorporate almost any type of constraint into a routing problem, and when the savings and improvement procedures are run, they see the infinite total cost and never make a route that violates the added constraint.

Every constraint on a single route enters Model 1 in the same way, by its route cost, and Table 1 lists those of this lecture. A constraint across routes, such as on the number of vehicles, is not a route cost and needs a model of its own.

Table 1: Route costs. A constraint on one route enters Model 1 by its route cost, infinity when the constraint is violated, so savings never selects the route; an objective, or a constraint across routes, needs a model of its own.

| Constraint | Route cost | Where |
|---|---|---|
| One route: a route cost | | |
| none | $TC(r)$ | Ex. 2(a) |
| capacity | $\infty$ if demand $> K$ (Eq. 1) | Ex. 1, 7 |
| weight and cube | $\infty$ if either is exceeded (Eq. 2) | Ex. 2(b), 5, 6 |
| maximum cost | $\infty$ if $TC(r) > TC_{\max}$ (Eq. 2) | Ex. 2(c), 2(d), 6, 7 |
| time windows | least time, by a scan | Ex. 4, 5, 7 |
| hours of service | $\infty$ past 11 h driving or 14 h on duty | Ex. 5(b), 10 |
| maximum wait | $\infty$ past its limit | Ex. 7 |
| load mixes | $\infty$ if a load mix exceeds $K$ (Eq. 5) | Ex. 3 |
| any other | $\infty$ if violated, a left turn say | |
| A model of its own | | |
| fewest routes | an objective, not modeled | |
| maximum routes | across routes, not modeled | |
| fewest vehicles | objective of Model 3, not solved | Sec. 3 |
| maximum vehicles | across routes, not modeled | |
| routes per vehicle | assigned after routing | Sec. 3 |

Example 1: Clarke-Wright savings with capacity

Determine the routes of Model 1 from a depot at node 1 to customers at nodes 2 to 6, with the costs of Ex. 5 in Lecture 5.2, customer demands of 8, 5, 4, 7 and 6, and a vehicle capacity of 15: the optimal routes by brute force, and the routes the Clarke-Wright savings procedure constructs, by hand and in Julia.

Example 1(a): By brute force

Determine the routes of least total cost that serve every customer within the capacity, by enumerating every way of dividing the customers among routes.

Node 1 is the depot, and nodes 2 to 6 are customers, with customer demands 8, 5, 4, 7 and 6, respectively, and the vehicle capacity is 15. The symmetric costs are those of Ex. 5 in Lecture 5.2. One listing of the example gives node 3 a demand of 3, where every other statement of it gives 5, which is used here; checking a number against the other statements of its data in this way is a Source check of Lecture 1.2, and the optimal routes are the same with either.

The demands are in units, which can be thought of as tons or cartons or whatever is delivered, and the vehicle can carry at most 15 units. The first step is to take the locations and put each customer’s demand next to it, so that it is easy to see, beside the costs between them.

The costs between the nodes are:

A set partition is a way of dividing a set of $n$ items into non-empty, disjoint subsets whose union is the original set. For example, if the set is $\{1, 2, 3\}$, the possible partitions are:

- [[1, 2, 3]] (one subset)
- [[1, 2], [3]], [[1, 3], [2]], [[2, 3], [1]] (two subsets)
- [[1], [2], [3]] (three subsets)

The total number of distinct partitions of a set with $n$ elements is given by the $n$-th Bell number, denoted $B_n$. For $n = 3$, $B_3 = 5$. Each partition of the customers is one way of dividing them among routes, a route for each subset.

With every constraint of Eq. 1 known from the start, the brute force is in the route cost itself: each way of dividing the customers among routes, each route visiting its customers in their least costly order, and the cost of a division in which some route is over capacity infinite. Code block 2 takes the divisions, the partitions of the customers, one at a time, keeps those in which every route fits, and ranks them by their total cost, the objective of Model 1:

```julia
# Code block 2: every partition into routes that fit, by brute force
using Combinatorics
Ccw = [ 0  40  48  38  33  48   # the costs of Ex. 5 of Lecture 5.2
       40   0  87  46  65  75
       48  87   0  67  41  47
       38  46  67   0  70  34
       33  65  41  70   0  69
       48  75  47  34  69   0]
K = 15                          # the vehicle's capacity
besttour(S) =                   # a route's customers in their best order
    minimum((sum(segcost([1; p; 1], Ccw)), [1; p; 1])
            for p in permutations(S))
BF = DataFrame(Vehicles = Int[], TC = Int[], Routes = String[])
for P in partitions(2:6)
    all(S -> sum(qcw[S]) <= K, P) || continue  # a route over capacity
    tours = besttour.(P)
    rs = ["(" * join(r, ",") * ")" for r in last.(tours)]  # as text
    push!(BF, (length(P), sum(first.(tours)), join(rs, " ")))
end
sort!(BF, :TC)                  # least TC first
@show length(partitions(2:6))   # the partitions looked at
@show nrow(BF)                  # those in which every route fits
prt(first(BF, 3))

```

- 1 Each order of a route’s customers is paired with its cost, and minimum compares the pairs by cost first, so it returns the least cost together with its order, as Code block 4 of Lecture 5.2 does for routes.
- 2 partitions(2:6), from the Combinatorics package, generates every partition of customers 2 to 6, one at a time. A partition divides a set into non-empty, disjoint subsets whose union is the set, so each P is one way of dividing the customers among routes, a vector of subsets such as [[2, 5], [3, 4, 6]], a route for each subset.

```text
length(partitions(2:6)) = 52
nrow(BF) = 28
  Vehicles   TC                       Routes
────────────────────────────────────────────
         2  305        (1,2,5,1) (1,3,6,4,1)
         3  313  (1,2,1) (1,3,6,4,1) (1,5,1)
         3  322  (1,2,1) (1,3,5,1) (1,4,6,1)
```

Of the 52 ways of dividing the five customers among routes, 28 fit the capacity. No single route can serve all five, whose demands total 30, so two vehicles is the fewest, and only one division into two routes fits: customers 2 and 5 on one route and 3, 4 and 6 on the other, each route’s load exactly 15. It is also the least costly division, at 305 against 313 for the next, with 3 vehicles.

By brute force, the optimal routes are $(1, 2, 5, 1)$ and $(1, 3, 6, 4, 1)$, two vehicles at a total cost of 305.

Example 1(b): By hand

Determine the routes Clarke-Wright constructs, pair by pair, refusing any join that would exceed the capacity.

The savings, by Eq. 8 in Lecture 5.2, are those of Table 1 in Lecture 5.2, taken in the same order, from 52 down to 1, by the same three rules of Lecture 5.2, Sec. 3, each now applied only without exceeding the capacity.

As without capacity, 4 and 6 form the first route by rule (1), and 3 and 6 are combined by rule (2), but every time a join is made, the route has to be checked to make sure it is still capacity feasible. The initial route of 4 and 6 has a total of 10, which is less than 15, so it is capacity feasible. When 3 is added, the route is right at 15, so it is essentially done: anything more would exceed the capacity of 15, and with the legs to and from the depot it is a finished route. The pair 3 and 5, the next greatest saving, is eliminated, since 3 is already on the finished route, and likewise 2 and 4, 3 and 4, 2 and 6, and 5 and 6. Not until 2 and 5, the only two left, with a saving of 8, is a route formed, and with nothing left, it is the second route.

Table 2 takes the pairs in that order, the load each join would make in its Load column:

| 9 | $(2, 3)$ | $40 + 48 - 87 = 1$ | $15 + 15 = 30 > 15$ | refused | |

Fig. 2 draws the starting state and the three joins. The two routes are each loaded to exactly 15.

Figure 2: Clarke-Wright on Ex. 1, the depot the tan square and each demand, a given number, in red: (a) the starting state, each customer served out and back (gray, dotted); (b) to (d) a frame per join of Table 2, its step numbered as the table’s row is, the routes in blue and the pair each joins in red.

The routes cost $38 + 34 + 47 + 48 = 167$ and $40 + 65 + 33 = 138$, a total of 305. Serving each customer out and back would cost $2(40 + 48 + 38 + 33 + 48) = 414$, and the three joins saved $52 + 49 + 8 = 109$ of it, and $414 - 109 = 305$, a Balance check: the savings of the pairs joined account for the whole difference. And 305 is the optimum of Ex. 1(a), a Landmark check: with capacity, as without it in Ex. 5 in Lecture 5.2, Clarke-Wright constructs the optimal routes here.

With a capacity of 15, Clarke-Wright joins customers 4 and 6 and adds 3, refuses every join that would exceed the capacity, and then joins 2 and 5, constructing the routes $(1, 4, 6, 3, 1)$ and $(1, 2, 5, 1)$, at 305, the optimum.

Example 1(c): In Julia

Determine the routes Logjam’s savings procedure constructs with the capacity in the route cost, and compare them and their savings with those of Ex. 1(a) and 1(b).

The functions Lecture 5.2 defined for routes are used here by the same names, and Code block 3 repeats them:

Show the functions of Lecture 5.2

```julia
# Code block 3: the route functions of Lecture 5.2
rtesegsum(r, x) =                  # each segment's sum of x on board
    cumsum(x[r] .* ifelse.(isorigin(r), 1, -1))[1:end-1]
function twoopt_rte(r, rTCh)       # 2-opt that keeps r a route
    rᵒ, TCᵒ = copy(r), rTCh(r)
    done = false
    while !done
        done = true
        for i = 1:length(r)-1, j = i+1:length(r)
            r′ = vcat(r[1:i-1], reverse(r[i:j]), r[j+1:end])
            all(>(0), rtesegsum(r′, ones(maximum(r′)))) || continue
            TC = rTCh(r′)
            if TC < TCᵒ
                rᵒ, TCᵒ = r′, TC
                done = false
                break
            end
        end
        r = copy(rᵒ)
    end
    return rᵒ, TCᵒ
end
rte2idx(r::AbstractVector{<:Integer}) = r[isorigin(r)]  # its shipments
rte2idx(R::AbstractVector{<:AbstractVector}) = rte2idx.(R)  # per route
```

```text
rte2idx (generic function with 2 methods)
```

Each customer’s demand is a shipment from the depot, so shipment $k$ is delivered to node $k + 1$, and a truck tr begins and ends each route at the depot, as in Ex. 6(d) in Lecture 5.2. Logjam’s rteTC computes a route’s cost but knows nothing of a capacity, so the capacity is added the way Sec. 1 adds any constraint, by a route cost of one’s own: Code block 4 computes a route’s cost with rteTC, and then sets the cost to infinity when the shipments on the route weigh more than the capacity K. It then constructs the routes by savings and improves each by 2-opt:

The savings and their order are those of Table 2, and the routes, at 138 and 167, those of the hand working and the brute force, a Triangulate check of the three. Logjam’s savings is not Clarke-Wright: it can insert a customer anywhere in a route, by minimum cost insertion, where Clarke-Wright joins only at a route’s ends; on these five customers the two arrive at the same routes. Table 3 sets the three methods side by side.

Table 3: The three methods of Ex. 1 on the same five customers and capacity.

| Method | Construction | Vehicles | Total cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brute force, Ex. 1(a) | every partition, best order of each route | 2 | 305 |
| Clarke-Wright, Ex. 1(b) | joins at route ends only, by hand | 2 | 305 |
| Logjam’s savings, Ex. 1(c) | minimum cost insertion anywhere | 2 | 305 |

Logjam’s savings, with the capacity in its route cost, constructs the routes $(1, 5, 2, 1)$ and $(1, 3, 6, 4, 1)$ at a total of 305, the routes of Ex. 1(a) and 1(b), the first in reverse.

A vehicle can have more than one capacity, and a route can have a limit of its own. With both, the route cost of Model 1 is:

$$
c(r) = \begin{cases}
TC(r), & \text{if } \displaystyle\sum_{i \in r} q_{ik} \le K_k,\ k = 1, \dots, m, \\
& \text{and } TC(r) \le TC_{\max} \\[6pt]
\infty, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
$$

where

- $q_{ik}$ = demand of customer $i$, in the units of capacity $k$
- $K_k$ = capacity $k$ of the vehicle
- $m$ = number of the vehicle’s capacities
- $TC_{\max}$ = maximum total cost of a route, a distance or a time.

Savings takes it as its $c(R)$ as it takes Eq. 1, and nothing else in Model 1 changes.

Example 2: Thirty NC customers

Determine the routes of Model 1 from a depot to 30 customers in North Carolina: (a) with no constraint, a single tour; (b) with a truck’s capacity in weight and in cube; (c) with the capacity and a maximum distance of 600 mi on each route, by a route cost of one’s own; and (d) with the same maximum by the truck’s own limit.

Example 2(a): No constraint

Determine the tour that savings and 2-opt construct from the depot through all 30 customers, and how it compares with the optimal tour.

The 30 shipments are those of Ex. 8 in Lecture 5.2, each with its own origin and destination.

To turn them into a TSP kind of problem, a depot is added: the ending location of shipment 1 is used as the depot for the problem, and the 30 shipments then have a total of 31 location points, the depot and the beginning points of the 30 shipments. That is the data set, with great circle distances as the distances.

Code block 6 reads the locations and the shipments, takes the ending location of shipment 1 as the depot and the beginning location of each shipment as a customer, and computes their road distances, great circle distances times the circuity factor 1.2 of Ex. 8 in Lecture 5.2; each customer’s delivery is then a shipment from the depot, and a truck tr begins and ends each route there. It prints the first five of the shipments: each is from the depot, b, to its customer, e, both numbered among the 31 points of X and D, with its weight q, in tons, and its density s, in lb/ft³:

```julia
# Code block 7: the depot and the customers on a map
function basemap(x, y; roads = false)  # makemap around the points, its
    # borders in gray, and its interstates faded behind them if roads;
    # close at the sides, tall enough to show the state's borders whole
    fig, ax = makemap(x, y; xexpand = 0.02, yexpand = 0.12,
                      doRoadbkgd = roads)
    for p in ax.scene.plots          # the state borders, drawn opaque;
        to_color(p.color[]).alpha < 1 && continue    # the roads are faded
        p.color, p.linewidth = (ink, 0.45), 1.5
    end
    return fig, ax
end
rtecols = [bluec, dcc, colorant"#c26a00", colorant"#7b3294", redc,
           colorant"#8c564b", colorant"#d6439a", colorant"#0f8f9e"]
rtecol(k) = rtecols[mod1(k, length(rtecols))]    # route k's color
function rtelabels!(ax, R, sh, X, tr, lab)  # each route's number at the
    # centroid of its stops, in its color; lab = (align, offset), one of
    # each a route, moves each clear of every line (placed by hand)
    n = length(R)
    al, off = something(lab, (fill((:center, :center), n),
                              fill((0, 0), n)))  # unplaced: centered
    c = [let loc = filter(!=(tr.b), rte2loc(r, sh, tr))  # not the depot
             (sum(X[loc, 1]) / length(loc), sum(X[loc, 2]) / length(loc))
         end for r in R]
    return text!(ax, first.(c), last.(c); text = string.(1:n),
                 color = rtecol.(1:n), font = :bold, fontsize = 13,
                 align = al, offset = off)
end
function fitmap!(fig, ax)  # the figure's height fitted to the map
    lim = ax.finallimits[]
    resize!(fig, 600,
            round(Int, 600 * lim.widths[2] / lim.widths[1]) + 10)
    return fig
end
function milabel!(ax, what, d)  # a distance, at the map's lower left
    s = commas(round(d, digits = 2))
    s = "$what: $(rpad(s, findfirst('.', s) + 2, '0')) mi"
    return text!(ax, 0.02, 0.03; text = s, space = :relative,
                 color = ink, fontsize = 13, font = :bold,
                 align = (:left, :bottom))
end
function depot!(ax, X)  # the depot, a tan square over everything
    return scatter!(ax, [X[1, 1]], [X[1, 2]]; marker = :rect,
                    color = colorant"#f2d9a0", strokecolor = ink,
                    strokewidth = 1.5, markersize = 13)
end
function vrpmap(R, sh, X, tr; lab = nothing)  # each route from the depot
    x, y = X[:, 1], X[:, 2]                     # and back, in its color
    fig, ax = basemap(x, y)
    for (k, r) in enumerate(R)
        loc = rte2loc(r, sh, tr)
        lines!(ax, x[loc], y[loc]; color = rtecol(k), linewidth = 1.2)
        legarrows!(ax, x[loc], y[loc]; color = rtecol(k), onmap = true,
                   size = 7, every = 2)
    end
    scatter!(ax, x[2:end], y[2:end]; color = ink, markersize = 4)
    depot!(ax, X)
    fitmap!(fig, ax)
    tp = length(R) > 1 ? rtelabels!(ax, R, sh, X, tr, lab) : nothing
    return fig, ax, tp                          # tp: the routes' numbers
end
fig, ax = basemap(X[:, 1], X[:, 2]; roads = true)
scatter!(ax, X[2:end, 1], X[2:end, 2]; color = ink, markersize = 5)
depot!(ax, X)
fitmap!(fig, ax)
```

The shipments now make a proper TSP kind of data set, in which every shipment starts at the depot. It is peddling, because every shipment is loaded at the depot and then delivered to its point, and the only reason to go back to the depot is the truck itself: after it delivers the last product to the last customer, it travels empty back. Collecting would be the opposite, with the 1s in the ending locations: the truck would travel empty to the first customer and then collect all the way to the last. Which of the two locations is the depot distinguishes peddling from collecting. The data also give each shipment’s density, its value and its annual demand, so the same data set can be used for many different things, such as finding the minimum total logistics cost; for the classic vehicle routing problem, all that is used is the density and, when there is a capacity, the quantity to be shipped, the amount shipped, say, tomorrow, where the annual demand is what is expected over the whole year. First the problem is solved as a TSP, an unconstrained tour with a cyclic route, constructing the route by savings and improving it by 2-opt. The route vector has a length of 60, because each of the 30 shipments has a pickup and a delivery.

With no constraint, the tour is a TSP tour through the depot and the 30 customers, so its distance can be judged against the optimal tour, which the formulation of Model 1 in Lecture 5.1 finds; Code block 9 repeats Lecture 5.1’s functions for it, and Code block 10 solves it, and computes the cost of the other extreme, every customer served out and back on a route of its own:

Show the functions of Lecture 5.1

```julia
# Code block 9: the TSP formulation of Lecture 5.1
using JuMP, HiGHS
function subtours(succ)                # the cycles of a successor vector
    S, seen = Vector{Vector{Int}}(), falses(length(succ))
    for k ∈ eachindex(succ)
        seen[k] && continue
        Sₖ, i = Int[], k
        while !seen[i]                 # follow the arcs back to k
            seen[i] = true
            push!(Sₖ, i)
            i = succ[i]
        end
        push!(S, Sₖ)
    end
    return S
end
function TSP(c)
    size(c, 1) == size(c, 2) ||        # assumption (a): each pair's cost
        error("arc costs must be a square matrix")
    V = 1:size(c, 1)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, x[i ∈ V, j ∈ V; i ≠ j], Bin)    # no arc i to i
    @objective(model, Min,
               sum(c[i, j] * x[i, j] for i ∈ V, j ∈ V if i ≠ j))
    @constraint(model, leave[i ∈ V],
                sum(x[i, j] for j ∈ V if j ≠ i) == 1)          # (a)
    @constraint(model, enter[j ∈ V],
                sum(x[i, j] for i ∈ V if i ≠ j) == 1)          # (b)
    set_silent(model)
    set_attribute(model, "mip_rel_gap", 0.0)
    rounds = []
    while true
        optimize!(model)
        termination_status(model) == JuMP.OPTIMAL ||
            error(termination_status(model))
        succ = [findfirst(j -> j ≠ i && value(x[i, j]) > 0.5, V)
                for i ∈ V]             # the node after each node
        S = subtours(succ)
        push!(rounds, (TC = objective_value(model), S = S))
        if length(S) == 1              # a single tour: done
            return (TC = objective_value(model), tour = [S[1]; S[1][1]],
                    rounds = rounds)
        end
        for Sₖ ∈ S                     # (c), for each subtour found
            @constraint(model,
                sum(x[i, j] for i ∈ Sₖ, j ∈ Sₖ if i ≠ j) ≤ length(Sₖ) - 1,
                base_name = "singletour")
        end
    end
end
```

Example 2(b): Capacity

Determine the routes with a truck that carries at most 25 tons and 2,750 ft³, first by a route cost of one’s own and then by a route cost that reads the truck’s capacity, and each route’s weight and cube.

Each customer’s shipment has a weight $q$, in tons, and a density $s$, in lb/ft³, in the data, and the truck’s capacity is added to tr, as Lecture 3.2 writes it. In Eq. 2 the truck has $m = 2$ capacities, its weight capacity $K_{wt}$ of 25 tons and its cube capacity $K_{cu}$ of 2,750 ft³, and a customer’s demands in their units are its shipment’s weight $q$ and its cube $2000q/s$. Logjam’s rteTC, though, does not read a capacity: Code block 12 adds the two to the shipments and the truck, and finds the tour of Ex. 2(a) over the cube capacity, while rteTC still returns its distance as its cost:

```julia
# Code block 12: Logjam's rteTC does not read a truck's capacity
sh.q, sh.s = sh0.q, sh0.s                # each shipment's weight, density

cu = 2000sh.q ./ sh.s                    # each shipment's cube, ft³
@show sum(sh.q[rte2idx(r1)])             # the tour's weight, t
@show sum(cu[rte2idx(r1)])               # and cube: more than 2,750
rteTC(r1, sh, D, tr)                     # a cost all the same
```

```text
sum(cu[rte2idx(r1)]) = 3795.3722254859936
```


With a weight capacity of 25 tons, the sum of the weights of a route’s shipments is checked against the truck’s capacity, and if it is less than or equal to it, the route is weight feasible. Doing a similar thing for $q/s$, the shipment’s weight over its density, times 2,000 pounds per ton, gives the route’s total cube, and checking it against the cube capacity tells whether the route is cube feasible. The route cost then returns the distance if the route is both weight and cube feasible, and otherwise infinity. Applying the savings procedure gives two routes, and each route’s distance, weight and cube can then be looked at; for these shipments, routes typically cube out before they weigh out, which is the most typical scenario. The neat thing is that the route cost can be defined however is wanted, to include whatever kind of constraints, and they carry over into the procedure: it is a flexible tool. Time windows would be the same: if the scan of a particular route found it infeasible, the route cost would return infinity, and the routing procedure would never create that route.

Code block 13 is the route cost of one’s own, which computes a route’s cost by rteTC and returns infinity unless the route’s shipments are within both capacities; savings and 2-opt then use it unchanged:

```julia
# Code block 13: capacity in a route cost of one's own
function rTDh(rte)
    rTD = rteTC(rte, sh, D, tr)
    idxsh = unique(rte)
    wtfeas = sum(sh.q[idxsh]) <= tr.Kwt
    cufeas = sum(2000sh.q[idxsh] ./ sh.s[idxsh]) <= tr.Kcu
    return wtfeas && cufeas ? rTD : Inf
end
@show rTDh(r1)                           # the tour: over capacity
R2 = [twoopt_rte(r, rTDh)[1] for r in savings(rTDh, sh)]
TD2 = rTDh.(R2)

```

With the constraint’s code in view, the same capacities can be read from the truck itself by a route cost that knows them, rteTC_vrp, which implements the route cost of Eq. 2. It takes the arguments of Logjam’s rteTC; for each segment of a route on which a different set of shipments is on board, it checks the weight and cube of those shipments against tr.Kwt and tr.Kcu; it checks the route’s total cost against a maximum, tr.maxTC; and it scans the route’s time windows, the subject of Sec. 2. Besides the cost, it returns an exit flag, 1 for a feasible route and a negative number naming the constraint an infeasible one violates (−1 not a single route, −2 weight, −3 cube, −4 maximum total cost, −5 a time window), and a table of the route’s stops:

Show the route cost rteTC_vrp

```julia
# Code block 15: rteTC_vrp, a route's cost, exit flag and schedule, with
# capacity, loading and unloading, a maximum cost and time windows
function rte2ldmx(rte)  # the shipments on board at each load mix
    isL, on, ld = isorigin(rte), Int[], Vector{Int}[]
    for i in 1:length(rte)-1
        isL[i] ? push!(on, rte[i]) : filter!(!=(rte[i]), on)
        isL[i] && !isL[i+1] && push!(ld, copy(on))  # a load mix
    end
    return ld
end

function rteTC_vrp(rte::AbstractVector{<:Integer}, sh, C, tr = (;))
    has(f) = hasproperty(sh, f)                 # a column of sh?
    col(f, v) = has(f) ? float.(sh[rte, f]) : fill(v, length(rte))
    isL, istr = isorigin(rte), haskey(tr, :b)   # truck's b and e?
    loc = rte2loc(rte, sh, istr ? tr : (b = [], e = []))
    Xflg = 1
    if istr && tr.b == tr.e        # back at the truck's location early:
        k = filter(!=(0), diff(loc[2:end-1] .== tr.b))  # two routes
        (length(k) > 2 || length(k) == 2 && k != [-1, 1]) && (Xflg = -1)
    end
    if Xflg > 0 && has(:q)                      # each load mix's
        for ld in rte2ldmx(rte)                 # weight and cube
            if haskey(tr, :Kwt) && sum(sh.q[ld]) > tr.Kwt
                Xflg = -2; break
            elseif haskey(tr, :Kcu) && 2000sum(sh.q[ld] ./ sh.s[ld]) >
                   tr.Kcu + 0.01sqrt(eps())     # a rounding tolerance
                Xflg = -3; break
            end
        end
    end
    Xflg < 0 && return Inf, Xflg, DataFrame()
    t = [k == 1 || loc[k] == loc[k-1] ? zero(eltype(C)) :
         C[loc[k-1], loc[k]] for k in eachindex(loc)]  # same place: 0
    tLU = ifelse.(isL, col(:tL, 0.0), col(:tU, 0.0))  # load, unload
    istr && (tLU = [0; tLU; 0])
    TC = foldl(+, t) + foldl(+, tLU)    # added in order, left to right
    haskey(tr, :maxTC) && TC > tr.maxTC && return Inf, -4, DataFrame()
    R = istr ? [0; rte; 0] : rte
    tw = (:tbmin, :tbmax, :temin, :temax)
    if !any(f -> has(f) || haskey(tr, f), tw)
        out = DataFrame(Rte = R, Loc = loc, Cost = t)  # no windows
        (has(:tL) || has(:tU)) && (out.LU = tLU)
        return TC, Xflg, out
    end
    lo = ifelse.(isL, col(:tbmin, -Inf), col(:temin, -Inf))  # windows
    hi = ifelse.(isL, col(:tbmax, Inf), col(:temax, Inf))
    if istr              # the truck's, also at stops at its b and its e
        lo = [get(tr, :tbmin, -Inf); lo; get(tr, :temin, -Inf)]
        hi = [get(tr, :tbmax, Inf); hi; get(tr, :temax, Inf)]
        c = [1; findall(diff(loc) .!= 0) .+ 1]  # where location changes
        n = length(loc)
        for (ix, j) in ((2:c[2]-1, 1), (c[end]:n-1, n))  # stops at b, e
            lo[ix] = replace(lo[ix], -Inf => lo[j])
            hi[ix] = replace(hi[ix], Inf => hi[j])
        end
    end
    TC, _, _, s = scanTW(t, tLU, lo, hi)        # Sec. 2's scan, its c
    isinf(TC) && return Inf, -5, DataFrame()
    isnan(TC) && (TC = sum(t) + sum(tLU))       # no window at all
    # the waits, from the schedule, none below 0 from rounding
    w = max.(0, [0; s[2:end] - s[1:end-1] - tLU[1:end-1] - t[2:end]])
    out = DataFrame(Rte = R, Loc = loc, Cost = t,
        Arrive = [0; s[2:end] - w[2:end]], Wait = w, TWmin = lo,
        Start = s, LU = tLU, Depart = s + tLU, TWmax = hi,
        Total = t + w + tLU)
    return TC, Xflg, out
end
function rteTC_vrp(R::AbstractVector{<:AbstractVector}, sh, C, tr = (;))
    v = [rteTC_vrp(r, sh, C, tr) for r in R]    # each route of R
    return first.(v), getindex.(v, 2), last.(v)
end
```

Example 2(c): Maximum distance by a route cost of one’s own

Determine the routes when, besides the capacity, no route may exceed 600 mi, by a route cost of one’s own around the route cost of Ex. 2(b).

The first constraint added to the unconstrained problem is a maximum route distance, and it is added by just redefining the route total cost. The route cost already defined calls the route total cost; to add a constraint, the new one calls it again, gets its value, and uses Julia’s ternary operator: if the value is within the maximum distance of 600 mi, it is returned, and if it exceeds 600, infinity is returned. That one change feeds into all of the pairwise savings and all of the procedures, and the infinity keeps them from creating any route that exceeds 600 mi: a route of three shipments might be combined at a total of 325 mi, but adding a fourth shipment in the middle could exceed 600, and the route cost then returns infinity. Passed to the savings procedure, the new route cost gives, almost by magic, routes that satisfy the constraint, without any change to the savings procedure itself: several routes instead of a single one. It is typical for most of the routes to be cut off at the constraint, and for the last to be a catch-all. Savings returns a vector of routes, a single route vector for the TSP but in general several for the VRP, while 2-opt is designed to operate on a single route, so 2-opt is called for each route in an array comprehension. Another type of improvement procedure, one not implemented here or used very much, would take the shipments of the route with the most slack, perhaps all of them, and put them in the other routes, eliminating a route; 2-opt only works on a single route, so it never reduces the number of routes, only the distance of each.

Code block 18 keeps the route cost of Ex. 2(b), with its capacity, as rTDh0, and wraps it in a route cost of one’s own that returns infinity for a route over the maximum distance:

```julia
# Code block 18: a maximum distance, by a route cost of one's own
rTDh0(rte) = rteTC_vrp(rte, sh, D, tr)[1]   # capacity, as Ex. 2(b)
maxdist = 600
function rTDh(rte)                    # my VRP constraint
    TC = rTDh0(rte)
    return TC > maxdist ? Inf : TC
end
R3 = [twoopt_rte(r, rTDh)[1] for r in savings(rTDh, sh)]
TD3 = rTDh.(R3)
Wt = [sum(sh.q[rte2idx(r)]) for r in R3]
Cube = [sum(cu[rte2idx(r)]) for r in R3]
prt(DataFrame(TD = TD3, Wt = Wt, Cube = Cube))
```

```text
─────────────────────────

2  526.54  8.92  1,541.52
3  175.14  1.58    465.54
```

The first route is cut off at 598.06 mi, just short of the 600 mi limit, and the last is the catch-all, at 175.14 mi; Fig. 6 draws the routes.

### Pickup and delivery

The more general situation than routing from a single depot is a route of pickups and deliveries. The one difficulty with such a route is what is on board. The first route of Fig. 7 picks up shipments 1, 2 and 3 and then drops off 3, 2 and 1, and the numbers beneath each segment are the shipments on board over it: after the first pickup just shipment 1, after the second 1 and 2, then all three, and then back to two and to one. There is just one peak, where all three shipments are on board, which is called a single load mix. The second route picks up 1 and 2, drops off 1, leaving 2 on board, picks up 3, leaving 2 and 3, and then has just 3 on board: there are two places with different mixes of loads, a first and a second load mix. With two load mixes, capacity cannot be looked at for all of the shipments as one aggregate. A different mix of shipments is on board over each, so the truck could be at capacity on one load mix and, because the shipments differ, at capacity a second time on the other, where all of the shipments together would be well past its capacity. So what has to be determined is which load mix reaches the maximum capacity, since the two are unlikely to be at capacity at the same time.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 21: the load mixes of two routes
let  # set in the lecture math's serif, as the insertion positions are
    fig = Figure(size = (380, 250), figure_padding = 4,
                 fonts = (; regular = Makie.MathTeXEngine.texfont()))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; aspect = DataAspect())
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    dy = 0.62  # a row's height
    # a route's stops along a rule, beneath each segment the shipments on
    # board, and a box around each load mix: a loading followed by an
    # unloading, where what is on board peaks
    function loadmix!(r, y0, cap)
        n, ld = length(r), isorigin(r)
        text!(ax, 2.0 .* (0:n-1), fill(y0, n); text = string.(r),
              fontsize = 16, color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
        lines!(ax, [-0.4, 2n - 1.6], [y0 - 0.45, y0 - 0.45]; color = ink,
               linewidth = 1)
        onboard(k) = sort(setdiff(r[1:k][ld[1:k]], r[1:k][.!ld[1:k]]))
        depth = maximum(length(onboard(k)) for k in 1:n-1)
        for k in 1:n-1                     # the segment after stop k
            s = onboard(k)
            ys = y0 - 0.95 .- dy .* (0:length(s)-1)
            text!(ax, fill(2k - 1.0, length(s)), ys; text = string.(s),
                  fontsize = 16, color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
            if ld[k] && !ld[k+1]           # a load mix, boxed
                poly!(ax, Rect(2k - 1.42, ys[end] - 0.36, 0.84,
                               y0 - 0.2 - ys[end] + 0.36);
                      color = :transparent, strokecolor = bluec,
                      strokewidth = 1.5)
            end
        end
        yb = y0 - 0.95 - dy * (depth - 1) - 0.5
        text!(ax, n - 1.0, yb; text = cap, fontsize = 15, color = ink,
              align = (:center, :top))     # its subcaption
        return yb
    end
    yb = loadmix!([1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1], 0.0, "(a) A single load mix")
    yb = loadmix!([1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3], yb - 1.3,
                  "(b) A first and a second load mix")
    xlims!(ax, -0.6, 10.6); ylims!(ax, yb - 0.6, 0.45)
    fig
end
```

Figure 7: Load mixes. Beneath each segment of a route are the shipments on board, and a box marks each load mix, where a loading is followed by an unloading: (a) the route $(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1)$ has a single load mix; (b) the route $(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)$ has a first and a second load mix.

What is on board changes only at a stop: a loading adds its shipment and an unloading removes it, as rtesegsum of Code block 3, from Lecture 5.2, adds them up. So the load on board over each segment of a route is a running sum:

$$
w_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \delta_j \, q_{r_j}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, 2n - 1
\tag{3}
$$

where

- $w_k$ = load on board over segment $k$, from stop $k$ to $k + 1$ (capacity units)
- $r_j$ = shipment loaded or unloaded at stop $j$ of route $r$
- $n$ = number of shipments on route $r$, each at two of its stops
- $\delta_j$ = sign of stop $j$
= $\begin{cases} +1, & \text{if stop } j \text{ loads shipment } r_j \\ -1, & \text{if it unloads it} \end{cases}$
- $q_i$ = size of shipment $i$, in the units of the capacity.

A load mix is what is on board at a peak of $w$, a segment $k$ whose stop $k$ is a loading and stop $k + 1$ an unloading. A shipment is on board over segment $k$ when it was loaded at or before stop $k$ and is unloaded after it, so the load mix at a peak $k$ is the set of those shipments:

$$
\ell_k = \{\, i : k_i^{+} \le k < k_i^{-} \,\}
\tag{4}
$$

where

- $k_i^{+}$ = stop of route $r$ at which shipment $i$ is loaded, where $\delta = +1$
- $k_i^{-}$ = stop at which shipment $i$ is unloaded, where $\delta = -1$.

Each shipment appears twice in a route, loaded where it first appears and unloaded where it appears again, and that gives each stop its sign $\delta_k$. For the second route of Fig. 7, $r = (1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)$, with each $q_i = 1$, Eq. 3 counts the shipments listed beneath each segment of the figure, each $w_k$ the one before it plus $\delta_k$, starting from 0:

$$
\begin{array}{l|rrrrrr}
k & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\
\hline
r_k \text{, shipment at stop } k & 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 3 \\
\delta_k & +1 & +1 & -1 & +1 & -1 & -1 \\
w_k \text{, over segment } k & 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 &
\end{array}

$$

A peak is a $+1$ followed by a $-1$, at segments 2 and 4. In Eq. 4, $k_i^{+}$ and $k_i^{-}$ are the two stops at which shipment $i$ appears in $r$, and the condition reads: loaded at or before stop $k$, $k_i^{+} \le k$, and not yet unloaded, $k < k_i^{-}$. At each peak, each shipment is checked:

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc|cc}
i & k_i^{+} & k_i^{-} & k = 2 & k = 4 \\
\hline
1 & 1 & 3 & 1 \le 2 < 3 & 1 \le 4 \nless 3 \\
2 & 2 & 5 & 2 \le 2 < 5 & 2 \le 4 < 5 \\
3 & 4 & 6 & 4 \nleq 2 < 6 & 4 \le 4 < 6 \\
\hline
\ell_k & & & \{1, 2\} & \{2, 3\}
\end{array}

$$

At the first peak, shipment 3 is not yet loaded, and at the second, shipment 1 has already been unloaded, so $\ell_2 = \{1, 2\}$ and $\ell_4 = \{2, 3\}$, the two boxes of Fig. 7 (b). The first route, $(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1)$, has $w = (1, 2, 3, 2, 1)$ and one peak, at segment 3, with all three shipments on board: $\ell_3 = \{1, 2, 3\}$. The load of a load mix is $\sum_{i \in \ell_k} q_i = w_k$, the load on board at its peak. Since $w$ rises only at a loading and falls only at an unloading, its largest values are at its peaks, so a route is within a capacity over every segment if and only if it is within it at each load mix.

A route from a depot, as in Ex. 1 and Ex. 2, loads every shipment before it unloads any, so it has a single load mix, and checking the weight and cube of all of a route’s shipments, as the route cost of one’s own of Ex. 2(b) does, is checking its one load mix. On a pickup and delivery route the two checks differ: rteTC_vrp checks each load mix, its function rte2ldmx listing the shipments on board at each peak.

The pickup and delivery problem, Model 2, is the load formation of Model 2 in Lecture 5.2 with a route cost, each shipment with its own origin and destination, and Model 1 is its special case in which every shipment is loaded at the depot. What changes from Lecture 5.2’s model is marked:

minimize: total cost of the routes and of the shipments shipped independently

solve for:
(a) shipments shipped independently, and the load of each route;
(b) route of each load, a sequence of stops, the loading and the unloading of each shipment on it.

subject to:
(a) Leave: each stop of a route is left exactly once, except the last;
(b) Enter: each stop of a route is entered exactly once, except the first;
(c) Single route: the arcs used by a route form one connected path through all its stops, not several, the truck carrying at least one shipment along each;
(d) Precedence: each shipment on a route is loaded before it is unloaded;
(e) Independent or consolidated: each shipment is on exactly one route or is shipped independently;
(f) Feasible routes: each route satisfies every constraint on a single route, such as the vehicle’s capacity over each load mix.

assumptions:
(a) each shipment has its own origin and destination;
(b) costs between locations are given and need not be symmetric;
(c) cost of a route is ~~the sum of the costs of its segments, from the loading of the first shipment to the unloading of the last~~ given by a route cost, the route’s distance or time from the loading of its first shipment to the unloading of its last when it is feasible, and infinity when it is not;
(d) one company owns every shipment;
(e) each shipment shipped independently costs its independent transport charge;
~~(f) each route’s truck has no capacity limit.~~

Model 2: Pickup and delivery problem

Generalization of Model 2: Load formation in Lecture 5.2

With a capacity on each load mix, as in Ex. 3, the route cost of Model 2 is a route’s total cost when the shipments on board over each load mix are within the capacity and infinity otherwise:

$$
c(r) = \begin{cases}
TC(r), & \text{if } \displaystyle\sum_{i \in \ell} q_i \le K \text{ for each load mix } \ell \text{ of } r \\[6pt]
\infty, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $r$ = route, its loadings and unloadings, as in Lecture 5.2
- $\ell$ = load mix of $r$, Eq. 4, the shipments on board at a peak of Eq. 3 (Fig. 7).

The other symbols are those of Eq. 3 and Eq. 1. The formulation of Model 2 is the savings procedure of Model 1, each route then improved by 2-opt, with the route cost as its $c(R)$ and the cost of a route of one shipment its independent charge, so that a shipment that savings leaves on a route of its own is shipped independently; Ex. 3 finds its loads both by brute force and by savings.

The savings procedure is the one normally used for the pickup and delivery problem. The key idea is that the savings are calculated relative to two shipments being shipped independently: what is saved if they are consolidated together. It tends to work better than minimum cost insertion when there are lots of constraints; as was seen in Lecture 5.2, for the unconstrained problem, randomized insertion worked better than randomized savings.

Example 3(a): By hand

Determine whether each route of Fig. 7 fits the truck, load mix by load mix, when each shipment weighs 10 tons.

Each route of the three shipments carries all three at some point, and they weigh 30 tons together, so a check of the whole route’s weight refuses every route. By Eq. 3, with $q_i$ the weight of shipment $i$, the weights on board over the five segments of the two routes of Fig. 7 are found by adding each stop’s weight at a loading and subtracting it at an unloading:

$$
\begin{array}{l|rrrrr}
\text{segment } k & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\
\hline
\text{route } (1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1)\text{:} \quad \delta_k q_{r_k} & +10 & +10 & +10 & -10 & -10 \\
w_k & 10 & 20 & 30 & 20 & 10 \\
\hline
\text{route } (1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)\text{:} \quad \delta_k q_{r_k} & +10 & +10 & -10 & +10 & -10 \\
w_k & 10 & 20 & 10 & 20 & 10
\end{array}

$$

The first route has one peak, at segment 3, where shipment 3 is loaded and then unloaded, and so one load mix, $\{1, 2, 3\}$; the second has two, at segments 2 and 4, $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$. Load mix by load mix, as in Eq. 5, with the capacity $K$ the truck’s weight capacity $K_{wt}$, the two routes are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1)&: \quad q_1 + q_2 + q_3 = 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 > 25 = K_{wt} \\
(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)&: \quad q_1 + q_2 = 10 + 10 = 20 \le 25, \\
&\phantom{:} \quad q_2 + q_3 = 10 + 10 = 20 \le 25
\end{aligned}

$$

The single load mix of the first route is over the capacity, and the route is infeasible; each of the two load mixes of the second fits, and the route is feasible, although the three shipments it carries weigh 30 tons in all.

At 10 tons each, the route $(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1)$, with one load mix of 30 tons, does not fit a truck of 25 tons, and the route $(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)$, with two load mixes of 20 tons, does.

Example 3(b): By brute force and by savings

Determine how many of the 60 routes of the three shipments fit load mix by load mix, and the least costly loads, by brute force and by savings.

Code block 24 takes the 60 routes of Ex. 1 in Lecture 5.2 one at a time, listing them as Code block 4 of Lecture 5.2 does (its notes 2 and 3 explain how), and computes the cost of each with rteTC_vrp, which returns infinity for a route with a load mix over the capacity; it gives the weights on board of Ex. 3(a)’s second route by rtesegsum, counts the routes that fit load mix by load mix, by the route cost and again by the peaks of Eq. 3, and those that would fit by the whole route’s weight, and finds the least costly route:

```julia
# Code block 24: all 60 routes, each load mix within 25 tons
v = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]
rtes = (r for r ∈ multiset_permutations(v, 6)       # the 60 routes
        if all(>(0), rtesegsum(r, ones(3))))
rTD3h(r) = rteTC_vrp(r, sh3, D3, tr3)[1]   # Inf if a load mix is over
@show rte2ldmx([1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1])         # its one load mix
@show rte2ldmx([1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3])         # its two load mixes
@show rtesegsum([1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3], sh3.q)  # on board, by segment
@show count(isfinite(rTD3h(r)) for r ∈ rtes)  # each load mix fits
@show count(maximum(rtesegsum(r, sh3.q)) <= tr3.Kwt for r ∈ rtes)
@show count(sum(sh3.q[unique(r)]) <= tr3.Kwt for r ∈ rtes)  # all fit
TC3ᵒ, r3ᵒ = minimum((rTD3h(r), r) for r ∈ rtes)
@show TC3ᵒ                                 # the cheapest route
r3ᵒ
```

The loads of Model 2 need not put all three shipments on one route: two can share a route with the third shipped independently, or all three can be shipped independently. Code block 25 computes the cost of those loads too, a shipment shipped independently costing its own distance, as in Ex. 2 in Lecture 5.2. That is the cost of its route of one shipment, so savings run with rTD3h, each route then improved by 2-opt, is the formulation of Model 2 as it stands, and Code block 25 runs it and compares its loads with the brute force’s:

```julia
# Code block 25: two on a route and one alone, all alone, and savings
indep(k) = rTD3h([k, k])                   # shipment k shipped alone
function pairplusone(i, j)                 # i and j on a route, k alone
    k = only(setdiff(1:3, [i, j]))
    rs = (r for r ∈ multiset_permutations([i, i, j, j], 4)
          if all(>(0), rtesegsum(r, ones(3))))
    return minimum(rTD3h(r) for r ∈ rs) + indep(k)
end
@show sum(indep(k) for k in 1:3)           # all three alone
TC3p = [pairplusone(i, j) for (i, j) in [(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)]]
@show TC3p                                 # 1 and 2, 1 and 3, 2 and 3
R3 =[twoopt_rte(r, rTD3h)[1] for r in savings(rTD3h, sh3)]  # savings
@show R3
R3 == [r3ᵒ]                                # the brute force's loads?
```

24 of the 60 routes fit load mix by load mix, the same by the route cost and by the peaks, where a check of the whole route’s weight would refuse all 60, and the least costly of them is the route $(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)$ of Ex. 3(a), at 849.11 mi, the route Lecture 5.2 found optimal without a capacity, a Landmark check: at 10 tons each, the capacity changes nothing. It is less than any load with a shipment shipped independently, and savings constructs the same route, a Triangulate check: two procedures, one answer.

At 10 tons each, 24 of the 60 routes fit, and the least costly loads, by brute force and by savings, are all three shipments on the route $(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3)$, at 849.11 mi.

## 2. Time windows

Why a route would have time windows can be seen in a dial-a-ride service, in which a van picks people up at their homes, typically elderly or disabled people who cannot drive, and takes them to places such as a doctor’s appointment. To be efficient, the van is not dedicated to one person’s transport but runs a multi-stop route that combines pickups with drop-offs, and each pickup has a guaranteed time window, usually about two hours or perhaps an hour, within which the van arrives.

One consideration with time windows is whether a vehicle may arrive early. If the window opens at 1 p.m. and the vehicle arrives at noon, it is usually still feasible for it to wait an hour, but in some cases there can be no waiting: the window has to be hit, and arriving early is another constraint. The windows of the VRP are absolute, a time of day such as 1 p.m., and a time-window constraint of this kind can be checked by a simple scanning procedure, so including it is not computationally difficult. Project scheduling also has time windows, but they are relative: once a task is complete, the next has to be done within one hour, perhaps because of some chemical process, and when the first will be done is not known in advance. A relative window cannot be checked by scanning; it has to be solved by a shortest path procedure with negative arcs, where Dijkstra’s procedure does not work and the Floyd-Warshall procedure is used.

Lecture 4.1, Sec. 3 introduced the relative windows, as the negative arcs of project scheduling that Dijkstra’s procedure cannot handle; the windows of vehicle routing are absolute instead, and a scan of the route checks them.

With time windows, the route cost of Model 1 is a route’s least time, its travel, unloading and waiting, and infinity when no schedule meets every window. It is found by scanning the route. The forward scan, a, starts at the opening of the window of the route’s first stop, the depot, and finds the earliest each stop can be served, waiting where a window has not yet opened; the last stop’s gives the earliest the route can finish. The reverse scan, b, goes back from that finish and finds the latest each stop can be served, the first stop’s giving the latest the route can start. The forward scan again, c, from that latest start, is the schedule, and the route’s least time is its earliest finish less its latest start.

Code block 28 does the three scans as scanTW, and rteTC_vrp of Ex. 2(b) calls it for any route with time windows:

```julia
# Code block 28: scanTW, the three scans of a route with time windows
function scanTW(t, u, ℓ, h)  # time-window scans: route time, a, b, c
    n = length(t)
    a = zeros(n); a[1] = ℓ[1]            # forward: the earliest start
    for k in 2:n
        a[k] = max(a[k-1] + u[k-1] + t[k], ℓ[k])  # wait if early
        a[k] + u[k] > h[k] && return Inf, a, a, a  # its window closed
    end
    b = zeros(n); b[n] = a[n]            # reverse: the latest start
    for k in n-1:-1:1
        b[k] = min(b[k+1] - t[k+1] - u[k], h[k] - u[k])
    end
    c = zeros(n); c[1] = b[1]            # forward again: the schedule
    for k in 2:n
        c[k] = max(c[k-1] + u[k-1] + t[k], ℓ[k])  # waits made late
    end
    return a[n] + u[n] - b[1], a, b, c   # earliest finish less start
end
```

```text
scanTW (generic function with 1 method)
```

The route’s windows are in hours of the day, $[0, 24]$ h; the loading/unloading time is 0; the vehicle’s capacity is $\infty$; and its lower bound, $LB = 5$ h, is the sum of its travel times. Its data are in Table 4.

| Stop | Travel time in (h) | Window (h) |
|---|---|---|
| 1, depot, departure | | [6, 18] |

Example 4(a): By hand

Determine the earliest finish, the latest start and the schedule by the three scans.

The time-window constraint takes a little more work than capacity, but computationally it is not very difficult. The route has a depot at node 1 and three customers, with travel times of 1, 2, 1 and 1 hours on its legs. There is assumed to be no time for loading or unloading the vehicle, which could be added but would only make the example more complicated, and the vehicle’s capacity is infinite, so there is no limit on it. The constraints are the time windows. Each customer has one: delivery to customer 2 can occur any time between 8 and 11, to customer 3 between 12 and 2 p.m., and to customer 4 between 3 and 6 p.m. The route is already set up to be close to feasible: if one window came before another in the direction the route travels, it would be known immediately to be violated. The depot itself has two windows, a departure window, any time between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., and a return window, between 6 p.m. and midnight. In practice the two do not overlap because of the distribution center itself: its loading docks are set up for receiving or for shipping out product, and there are many practical reasons not to mix the two. The question is the total time the route requires, and the objective is to minimize it. Its lower bound is 5 hours: with zero loading and unloading time, the lower bound is just the sum of the travel times, and even with no time windows the route would take at least 5 hours. With the windows, the question is the minimum time in which every customer can be served without violating a window, which may require the vehicle to pause when it arrives early until the window starts, as a truck waiting outside the customer’s location: arriving at 7 a.m. for a window that opens at 8 means waiting an hour. The route is solved by a series of scans. The first is a forward scan, which starts at the beginning of the departure window, 6 a.m., to give the best chance of realizing the minimum time. The vehicle arrives at customer 2 at 7 a.m. and, because of its window, waits one hour; with zero unloading time, at 8 it heads for customer 3, which takes two hours, arriving at 10 a.m., where the window starts at 12, so it waits two hours. At 12 it travels an hour to customer 4, arriving at 1 p.m., and waits two hours until 3; one hour back to the depot, it arrives at 4 and has to wait until 6 p.m. Were there a loading or unloading time, at a customer the unloading usually has to be within the window, while at the distribution center, for a peddling route, the loading can usually be done before the window starts, and unloading likewise outside it. What the first forward scan establishes is that the earliest the route can finish is 6 p.m., and that is not going to change. Starting at 6 a.m. and finishing at 6 p.m., though, the route spends twelve hours on the road, which is not as short as it could be. Since it has to finish by 6 p.m., the latest it can start is found by going in the backward direction. Reversing from 18, one hour back to customer 4 gives 17, within its window, so there is no waiting at that customer, which already saves time. One hour back to customer 3 gives 16, against a window that closes at 14, a two-hour wait; two hours back to customer 2 gives 12, against its close of 11, a one-hour delay; and one hour back to the depot gives 10. That is the latest start.

Fig. 10 draws the three scans, and Table 5 gives the equation of each step:

Figure 10: Ex. 4 by hand, a frame per scan, the depot the tan square with its departure window above it and its return window below: (a) the route as given; (b) the forward scan, from the earliest departure, each stop’s start after the time it is reached where the two differ; (c) the reverse scan, from the earliest finish, each stop’s latest start after the time it is reached going back; (d) the forward scan again, from the latest start, the waits as late as the windows allow. The arrow in the middle of each scan is its direction. Given values, the travel times and windows, are red; determined ones are blue.

Table 5: Ex. 4 by hand, the three scans with no unloading time ($u_k = 0$): the forward scan from the top, the reverse scan from the bottom, and the forward scan again from the top.

| Stop | Window | Forward $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{a}_k = \max\lbrace\mathrm{a}_{k-1} + t_k, \ell_k\rbrace}$ | Reverse $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{b}_k = \min\lbrace\mathrm{b}_{k+1} - t_{k+1}, h_k\rbrace}$ | Forward again $\boldsymbol{\mathrm{c}_k = \max\lbrace\mathrm{c}_{k-1} + t_k, \ell_k\rbrace}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1, depart | $[6, 18]$ | $\mathrm{a}_1 = 6$ | $\min\{11 - 1, 18\} = 10$ | $\mathrm{c}_1 = \mathrm{b}_1 = 10$ |
| 2 | $[8, 11]$ | $\max\{6 + 1, 8\} = 8$ | $\min\{14 - 2, 11\} = 11$ | $\max\{10 + 1, 8\} = 11$ |
| 3 | $[12, 14]$ | $\max\{8 + 2, 12\} = 12$ | $\min\{17 - 1, 14\} = 14$ | $\max\{11 + 2, 12\} = 13$ |
| 4 | $[15, 18]$ | $\max\{12 + 1, 15\} = 15$ | $\min\{18 - 1, 18\} = 17$ | $\max\{13 + 1, 15\} = 15$ |
| 1, return | $[18, 24]$ | $\max\{15 + 1, 18\} = 18$ | $\mathrm{b}_5 = \mathrm{a}_5 = 18$ | $\max\{15 + 1, 18\} = 18$ |

where

- $t_k$ = travel time into stop $k$ (h)
- $\ell_k$ = opening of the window of stop $k$ (h of the day)
- $h_k$ = closing of the window of stop $k$ (h of the day)
- $u_k$ = unloading time at stop $k$ (h)
- $\mathrm{a}_k$ = earliest stop $k$ can be served, by the forward scan
- $\mathrm{b}_k$ = latest stop $k$ can be served, by the reverse scan
- $\mathrm{c}_k$ = time stop $k$ is served in the schedule, by the forward scan again.

The earliest finish of the forward scan and the latest start of the reverse scan give the least time of the route:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Earliest Finish} - \text{Latest Start} = 18 - 10 &= 8 \text{ hr} \\
&= 5 \text{ travel} + 3 \text{ delay}
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
$$

The 8 hours of Eq. 6 are the 5 of travel, the lower bound, and the 3 of waiting the windows force, an hour at customer 4 and two at the depot in the last scan: a Balance check of Lecture 1.2, the travel and the waits accounting for the whole route. Read scan by scan:

The first forward scan takes $18 - 6 = 12$ hours, with 7 hours of wait, so 18 is the minimum finish time. The backward scan takes $18 - 10 = 8$ hours, with 3 of wait, so 10 is the maximum start time, and $18 - 10 = 8$ is the minimum total time for the route. The second forward scan has the same time and waits, but with the waits shifted to the end of the route, which is better in case something changes during route delivery.

The forward and reverse scans give exactly the information wanted: the route needs 3 hours of delay, and in the reverse scan’s schedule the delay is one hour at customer 2 and two hours at customer 3, with none at customer 4. Suppose the two scans are coded for a trucking company whose scheduler has been routing a dozen trucks by hand on a big piece of paper in a conference room, and with two or three dozen trucks can no longer keep track of them, its windows more complex than these, some customers served every Monday and others every second Monday. Given feasible, optimal routes, a scheduler can answer that they are really good, but that no truck would ever be routed like that. Nothing is wrong with the time: no route can do better than 8 hours. A third scan, a second forward scan, fixes it. The forward scan gave the earliest finish, 18; starting from it, the reverse scan gave the latest start, 10; the last forward scan, starting at 10, moves the delays from the beginning of the route to its end. The truck reaches customer 2 at 11 and customer 3 at 13 with no delay, and has only one hour of delay at the last customer and two hours back at the depot. Delays are better late, because something can happen, a truck breaking down, say; delays held for later are a safety stock of delay, and with them as late as possible, the windows are still satisfied if anything goes wrong. Taking them early is like eating all of a trip’s food in the first hour and hoping to arrive on time, where it is better to keep a sandwich or two in the backpack in case of a delay. Practicality is as important as optimality: a perfectly deterministic world does not map to the real world, where things happen, and showing a solution to someone who actually does the work, to see whether it passes the smell test as feasible, is how such knowledge is found.

The route takes at least 8 hours, 5 of travel and 3 of waiting: it leaves the depot at 10 and returns at 18, waiting an hour at customer 4 and two hours at the depot.

TC5 is 8.0 and Xflg5 is 1, a feasible route. The Start column where the truck moves, rows 1 and 5 to 8, is the c row of Code block 29, and the Total column sums to 8: the hand scans, scanTW and the route cost agree, a Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2.

In code, the same route needs a time matrix, just like a distance matrix, since it deals with time instead of distance: a 4 × 4 matrix with the known travel times put in. The shipments all begin at location 1, the depot, and end at locations 2, 3 and 4. The unloading time is 0, and the windows are given as the earliest and the latest time for delivery to each customer, 8, 12 and 15 and 11, 14 and 18. The truck carries over the truck of freight transport, but instead of its rate it uses fields for its beginning and end points, here both the depot; they carry over to multi-stop routes, in which a truck can start at any location and end at any other. A customer has just one window, an ending window, since it wants its delivery during a window, but the depot has both a beginning and an ending window, 6 to 18 and 18 to 24. The route is fixed in advance: shipments 1, 2 and 3 are dropped off in turn. Since ending windows are given for the customers, the example is peddling: every item is on the truck when it leaves the depot, and the three are dropped off at the customers. For collecting, the truck would leave the depot empty, pick up the three items and return them to the depot, and beginning windows would be given, since the pickup begins a shipment at a particular time. Whether the beginning or the ending windows are given shows whether a route is peddling or collecting. The route cost is called with the route, the shipment and truck information and the time matrix, which it uses to determine the total time of the route. Its second output is a flag giving the feasibility of the route, and its third a table of everything that happens on the route. Its route vector has a 0 at both ends for the depot, and in its location vector every shipment starts at location 1, the depot, and is delivered, which again shows a peddling route; for collecting, the end of the location vector would be all 1s. With no unloading time, a vehicle departs as soon as it arrives unless a window delays it. The route cost implements the forward scan, the reverse scan and then the forward scan again, putting the delays as far toward the end of the route as possible: an hour at the last customer and two hours back at the depot, the same as by hand. The route’s total time is the sum of the last column, 8, the total cost the route cost returns. The route cost does all the heavy lifting, and this is for just one route.

Of the six orders in which the three customers could be served, Code block 31 computes the cost of each, one at a time:

```julia
for p in permutations(1:3)        # deliver to the stops in order p
    TCp, Xflgp = rteTC_vrp([p; p], sh5, T5, tr5)[1:2]
    push!(P6, (join(p, ", "), TCp, Xflgp))
end
prt(P6)
```

```text
  2, 3, 1  Inf    -5
  3, 1, 2  Inf    -5
  3, 2, 1  Inf    -5
```

Only the order of the route is feasible, and every other is refused for a window (flag −5). The data of Ex. 4 give travel times only on the legs of its route, but no others are needed: its three windows do not overlap, so no route can satisfy them in any other order, whatever the other legs take.

In Julia, as by hand, the route takes 8 hours, leaving at 10 and returning at 18, its waits an hour at customer 4 and two at the depot; it is the only order of the three customers that satisfies every window.

Example 5: Thirty NC customers with time windows

Determine the routes of Model 1 from the depot of Ex. 2 to its 30 customers, the first 15 with a delivery window from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. and the other 15 from 1 p.m. to 11 p.m., at 50 mph with five minutes of positioning at each stop and 30 minutes of unloading a ton, within the windows, the truck’s capacity and the hours of service of Lecture 3.2, and the schedule of each.

Example 5(a): Windows, unloading and capacity

Determine the routes and schedules that the route cost with the windows, unloading times and capacity gives, and whether each is within the hours of service.

The depot and the customers are those drawn in Fig. 3.

The same can be done for the 30 shipments of Ex. 2. A travel time matrix is defined just as for the route of Ex. 4: the distance matrix, in miles, is converted to time at an average travel speed, and a positioning time is added at each stop, the time for the truck to get into position to make a pickup or delivery, beyond the time it is moving, here five minutes. The unloading time at each customer is proportional to the size of its shipment, 30 minutes a ton, so that it recognizes the amount delivered. The first 15 customers have daytime delivery, any time between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m., and the other 15 evening delivery, any time between 1 p.m. and 11 p.m. The truck itself has no time windows, so there is no restriction on when it can leave the depot or return to it; it has only its beginning and end points and its capacity. The routing is peddling, with deliveries only at the customers, and the same code as before solves it, the shipment and truck information encoded in the route cost. The schedule of each route gives when its vehicle departs the depot, when it arrives at each customer, any waiting time, and so on. Of particular interest in judging the quality of a routing solution is the waiting time, and here no route requires its vehicle to wait for a window, because the windows are very wide, basically the daylight hours against the evening; with narrow windows of an hour or two, positive waiting would likely be required, and quite different solutions would result.
