```julia
# Code block 35: the routes on a map
function twmap(R, TT; lab = nothing)  # depot routes, each its color and
    x, y = X[:, 1], X[:, 2]             # number, hours at the left
    col = rtecol.(eachindex(R))                    # Code block 7
    fig, ax = basemap(x, y)                        # Code block 7
    for (i, r) in enumerate(R)             # each route, depot to depot
        loc = rte2loc(r, sh, tr)
        lines!(ax, x[loc], y[loc]; color = col[i], linewidth = 1.2)
        legarrows!(ax, x[loc], y[loc]; color = col[i], onmap = true,
                   size = 8)
    end
    # the daytime customers filled, the evening ones open
    scatter!(ax, x[2:16], y[2:16]; color = ink, markersize = 6)
    scatter!(ax, x[17:31], y[17:31]; color = :white, strokecolor = ink,
             strokewidth = 1.2, markersize = 6)
    depot!(ax, X)                                  # Code block 7
    fitmap!(fig, ax)
    rtelabels!(ax, R, sh, X, tr, lab)              # Code block 7
    hrs(v) = "$(round(v, digits = 2)) h"
    for (i, h) in enumerate(TT)
        text!(ax, 0.02, 0.03 + 0.065 * (length(TT) - i + 1);
              text = "Route $i: " * hrs(h), space = :relative,
              color = col[i], fontsize = 13, align = (:left, :bottom))
    end
    text!(ax, 0.02, 0.03; text = "Total: " * hrs(sum(TT)),
          space = :relative, color = ink, font = :bold, fontsize = 13,
          align = (:left, :bottom))
    return fig
end
```

Example 5(b): Hours of service by a route cost of one’s own

Determine the routes and schedules when, besides the windows, unloading and capacity, each route is within the hours of service.

The route cost has no hours-of-service limit, so it is added by a route cost of one’s own, as in Sec. 1: Code block 37 calls rteTC_vrp, reads the driving time from its schedule, and sets the cost to infinity when the driving exceeds 11 hours or the route’s time on duty exceeds 14:

```julia
# Code block 37: hours of service, a wrapper that reads the schedule
function rTTh(rte)                 # hours of service (Lecture 3.2)
    TT, _, out = rteTC_vrp(rte, sh, T, tr)
    isinf(TT) && return Inf
    drive = sum(out.Cost)          # time at the wheel
    return drive > 11 || TT > 14 ? Inf : TT   # 11 h in a 14 h day
end
R6h = [twoopt_rte(r, rTTh)[1] for r in savings(rTTh, sh)]
TT6h = rTTh.(R6h)

```

- 1 out.Cost is the travel time into each stop, and the travel times T of Code block 32 carry the five minutes of positioning at each stop, so the 11 hours of driving include that positioning as well as the time the wheels are turning.

## 3. Routes to vehicles

In practice, as in the operational VRP of Model 3 in Lecture 1.1, the VRP minimizes the number of vehicles first. It is stated so in Model 3, which differs from Model 1 in its objective alone, marked:

minimize: first the number of vehicles used, then, among the solutions that use the fewest, the total cost of the routes

solve for:
(a) routes, each a sequence of customers that begins and ends at the depot.

subject to:
(a) Leave: each customer is left exactly once;
(b) Enter: each customer is entered exactly once;
(c) Routes: the arcs used form cycles, each passing through the depot;
(d) Feasible routes: each route satisfies every constraint on a single route, such as the vehicle’s capacity, a maximum distance or time, or time windows.

assumptions:
(a) arc costs are given and need not be symmetric;
(b) cost of a route is given by a route cost, the route’s distance or time when it is feasible and infinity when it is not.

Model 3: Vehicle routing problem

Restriction of Model 1: Vehicle routing from a depot

No procedure in this lecture solves Model 3. Savings, Clarke-Wright among them, is a construction, and 2-opt then improves each route only within itself: nothing tries to reduce the number of routes once they are constructed, and the number of vehicles is only a byproduct of how many routes savings constructs. So Model 3 is neither formulated nor implemented here. What is solved instead is the simpler Model 1, whose objective is the cost of the routes alone, and this section minimizes the number of vehicles only for routes already constructed.

Any kind of commercial package would minimize the number of vehicles. A more complicated type of improvement heuristic would typically be used, which goes beyond what this lecture takes up. The better approach in practice is the randomization of Lecture 5.2: the routes are constructed and improved by 2-opt many times, each time differently, in the hope of different results, and the best is kept in terms of the number of vehicles or routes, not their cost. It can be a much easier way of implementing that objective than trying to develop special-purpose improvement procedures for reducing the number of routes or vehicles, which is quite difficult. This is similar to bin packing, where randomization is typically better than more sophisticated improvement.

Once the routes are calculated, the question is the minimum number of trucks needed. A driver is assigned to a truck and is not restricted to doing one route a day, especially a route of an hour or less, unless, for example, a union contract allows only one; with any kind of flexibility, which most companies have, the first concern in a VRP is to minimize the number of trucks and drivers needed, and then to use them as much as possible during their ten hours. When loading at the distribution center (DC) takes a fixed time, irrespective of the size of the load, that time can be added to each route’s total time, and several routes can then be added together on one truck: a first route of three hours with its loading ends back at the DC, where the truck is loaded for another, so that two, three or perhaps four routes fit in the ten hours. That is really the major objective. Minimizing the time of the routes tends to give pretty good routes, but it is usually not what a company is most interested in: it would much rather spend an extra hour if that eliminates a truck, since saving one hour is not nearly as beneficial as saving one truck, and routes constructed to minimize time are constructed without that in mind. A commercial solution would add improvement procedures that move a shipment from one route to another: if three routes would fit in ten hours except that the last customer puts them over, that customer could go on another route, increasing the total time a little but eliminating the need for a truck. Determining the minimum number of trucks is essentially a bin packing problem, the problem of determining the minimum number of bins needed for a set of items: each route is an item, its time is its size, and the bins have a fixed size, here ten hours. A problem small enough can be done by hand, and bin packing gives an easy heuristic way to think about it.

Bin packing is the model of Model 6 in Lecture 2.7, with the routes as its objects, each route’s time as an object’s volume $v_j$, and a truck’s day as the volume $V$ of a bin. Lecture 2.7 solved it as a MILP; a heuristic constructs a packing directly:

In bin packing, objects (e.g., boxes) with different volumes v are packed into bins, each of volume V, in a way that tries to minimize the number of bins used. Given each object in arbitrary order, one straightforward algorithm, termed firstfit, is to place the object in the first bin that it fits into; if it does not fit into any bin, put it into a new bin. The following function returns an array where each element is the indices of objects from v in a bin. Each element of v is the volume of the object, and each bin is packed so that its total volume of objects does not exceed V:

```julia
# Code block 39: first fit
function firstfit(v, V)
    # Put first object into first bin
    B = [[1]]                               # Array of arrays
    b = [v[1]]                              # Array of scalars

    # Add remaining objects to bins
    for i = 2:length(v)
        idx = findfirst(b .+ v[i] .<= V) # Find first bin object fits into

        if idx !== nothing                  # Found existing bin
            b[idx] += v[i]
            push!(B[idx], i)
        else                                # Create new bin for object
            push!(b, v[i])
            push!(B, [i])
        end
    end

    return B
end
```

```text
firstfit (generic function with 1 method)
```

A variation of first fit, instead of taking the objects in a random order, orders them, and what typically works well in practice is to order them by decreasing size: all of the objects are ordered in decreasing size, and then the first fit procedure is applied, which in many cases does better than taking them at random. For some bin packing problems not all of the objects are at hand, so they cannot be sorted. These are called online problems: every hour, say, different objects arrive and a decision has to be made where each goes, so the largest is never seen among all of them, and an online procedure is needed. In an offline problem all of the objects are at hand and can be sorted, and then sorting in decreasing volume and applying first fit is probably the effective procedure. Whether a problem is online or offline can dictate which heuristic is even feasible, and which of those is the most effective.

The routes of a day are all constructed before any is assigned to a truck, so assigning them is an offline problem, and first fit applied to the routes in decreasing order of time is first-fit decreasing. Code block 40 sorts the objects largest first, packs them by firstfit, and returns each bin’s objects by their own indices:

```julia
# Code block 40: first-fit decreasing
function ffd(v, V)                     # first fit, largest first
    p = sortperm(v, rev = true)        # the objects, decreasing
    return [p[B] for B in firstfit(v[p], V)]  # their own indices
end
```

```text
ffd (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 6: Osborn’s routes to trucks

Osborn, Inc., is a company that supplies 45 customers each day from its DC in Detroit, Michigan, by tractor-trailer. Determine its routes, each within a 10-hour day, and the fewest trucks that can run them, by hand and in Julia.

Osborn, Inc., has a DC in Detroit, MI that supplies 45 customers each day with cases of different products using tractor-trailers. Customer location, load density (in lb/ft³), and weight (in lb) of each load for each customer are in the file osborn-detroit.csv. A load can be split between multiple trucks. The file includes the location of the depot (customer 1). Each identical truck must start and complete its route between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m., including travel and unloading time. Each truck requires 20 minutes for loading at the depot. It can be loaded at the depot before 7 a.m., and this loading time should not be included in the 10-hour total, but if the truck is used for more than a single route, the 20 minutes should be included in the 10-hour total. Unloading at each customer takes five minutes for positioning the truck and five minutes per ton of the load.

Each identical truck can carry a maximum of 2,750 ft³ and 25 tons. Each vehicle travels at an average speed of 35 mph and actual road distances can be estimated from great circle distances, times the circuity factor of 1.2 of Lecture 2.2, Sec. 7.

Example 6(a): Routes

Determine the routes, each within the truck’s capacity and the 10 hours, and each route’s time, weight and cube.

Code block 41 reads the customers, builds the truck, with the 10 hours as its maximum route cost, and splits any load larger than a truckload, as the statement allows: whole truckloads are split off as loads of their own, and the rest is kept. A truckload of a load is the most its density lets the trailer carry, maxpayld of Lecture 3.2. Each load’s unloading time is 5 minutes plus 5 minutes a ton:

```julia
# Code block 41: Osborn's customers, their loads, the truck
dfo = CSV.read("data/osborn-detroit.csv", DataFrame)
XYo = hcat(dfo.Longitude, dfo.Latitude)       # row 1 is the DC
To = 1.2dists(XYo, XYo, :mi) / 35             # h, at 35 mph
tro = (b = 1, e = 1, Kwt = 25, Kcu = 2750, maxTC = 10)
sho = DataFrame(b = 1, e = 2:nrow(dfo), q = dfo.Weight[2:end] / 2000,
                s = dfo.Density[2:end])
for i in findall(sho.q .> maxpayld.(eachrow(sho), Ref(tro)))
    qmax = maxpayld(sho[i, :], tro)           # a truckload of it
    for _ in 1:floor(Int, sho.q[i] / qmax)    # split off whole loads
        push!(sho, (b = 1, e = sho.e[i], q = qmax, s = sho.s[i]))
    end
    sho.q[i] = rem(sho.q[i], qmax)            # and keep the rest
end
sho.tU = 5/60 .+ 5sho.q / 60                  # 5 min, + 5 min a ton
prt(sho[sho.e .== sho.e[end], :])             # the load that was split
```

Example 6(b): Routes to trucks by hand

Determine the trucks the routes need, by first-fit decreasing on the route times, and the fewest trucks any assignment could use.

The times of the routes of Ex. 6(a), to two decimals, are $t_1, \ldots, t_{10}$ = 7.11, 5.03, 2.50, 2.32, 3.27, 0.92, 4.12, 3.77, 1.65 and 1.61 hours. A truck’s first route needs no loading in its day, and each later route adds its 20 minutes, $t_L = 0.33$ hours, so a truck can run the routes $B$ if

$$
\sum_{j \in B} t_j + t_L \left(\lvert B \rvert - 1\right) \le 10
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{j \in B} \left(t_j + t_L\right) \le 10 + t_L
\tag{7}
$$

where

- $B$ = set of routes a truck runs in its day
- $t_j$ = time of route $j$ (h)
- $t_L$ = loading time at the depot before each route after a truck’s first (h).

This is bin packing with each route’s volume $v_j = t_j + t_L$ and each truck’s $V = 10 + t_L$. First-fit decreasing takes the routes longest first and puts each on the first truck whose day Eq. 7 still allows, in Table 6:

Table 6: First-fit decreasing on the route times of Ex. 6(a): each route, longest first, on the first truck whose day stays within 10 hours, the day being the truck’s first route plus 0.33 hours and the time of each later route.

| Step | Route | $\boldsymbol{t_j}$ | Truck | Its day |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 7.11 | 1 (new) | $7.11$ |
| 2 | 2 | 5.03 | 2 (new) | $5.03$, since truck 1: $7.11 + 0.33 + 5.03 = 12.47 > 10$ |
| 3 | 7 | 4.12 | 2 | $5.03 + 0.33 + 4.12 = 9.48$, since truck 1: $11.56 > 10$ |
| 4 | 8 | 3.77 | 3 (new) | $3.77$, since truck 1: $11.21$, truck 2: $13.58$ |
| 5 | 5 | 3.27 | 3 | $3.77 + 0.33 + 3.27 = 7.37$, since truck 1: $10.71$ |
| 6 | 3 | 2.50 | 1 | $7.11 + 0.33 + 2.50 = 9.94$ |
| 7 | 4 | 2.32 | 4 (new) | $2.32$, since truck 3: $7.37 + 0.33 + 2.32 = 10.02 > 10$ |
| 8 | 9 | 1.65 | 3 | $7.37 + 0.33 + 1.65 = 9.35$ |
| 9 | 10 | 1.61 | 4 | $2.32 + 0.33 + 1.61 = 4.26$ |
| 10 | 6 | 0.92 | 4 | $4.26 + 0.33 + 0.92 = 5.51$ |

Step 7 is the near miss: route 4 would bring truck 3’s day to 10.02 hours, just over the 10. No assignment can use fewer trucks than the total volume of the routes over the volume of one truck, rounded up, the bound of Ex. 8 in Lecture 2.7:

$$
\Biggl\lceil \frac{\sum_j \bigl(t_j + t_L\bigr)}{10 + t_L} \Biggr\rceil
= \Biggl\lceil \frac{32.30 + 10(0.33)}{10.33} \Biggr\rceil
= \lceil 3.45 \rceil = 4

$$

so the 4 trucks of first-fit decreasing are the fewest possible, a Bounds check of Lecture 1.2. The bound is the minimum count of Lecture 1.3, Sec. 5, with no variability: the hours of work in a day over the hours one truck can work, rounded up.

A lower bound can be calculated for these problems, and sometimes the answer a heuristic gives is the lower bound: when it is equal to the lower bound, the heuristic solution can be said to be the globally optimal solution. When the number of bins exceeds the lower bound, all that can be said is that it is the best found, since not every lower bound is achievable, and even the global optimum can sometimes be above it, so the bound is not a guarantee; a heuristic solution above the lower bound is just the best-known solution.

First-fit decreasing puts the ten routes on 4 trucks, routes 1 and 3 on one, 2 and 7 on another, 8, 5 and 9 on a third, and 4, 10 and 6 on the fourth, which is the bound, so no assignment uses fewer.

By Little’s Law of Lecture 1.3, Sec. 3, the 34.3 truck-hours of the day, the routes and the loading before each truck’s later routes, over the 10 hours of a day are the trucks busy on average, 3.43, so at least 4 trucks are needed, as the bound says. Code block 48 repeats the bin packing model of Lecture 2.7, and Code block 49 finds the fewest trucks with it:

Show the bin packing of Lecture 2.7

```julia
# Code block 48: the bin packing model of Lecture 2.7
function binpack(v, V; tlim = 60.0, gap = 1e-4)
    M = 1:length(v)
    bp = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(bp)
    set_time_limit_sec(bp, tlim)           # give up after this long
    set_attribute(bp, "mip_rel_gap", gap)  # or once this close
    @variable(bp, y[M], Bin)
    @variable(bp, x[M, M], Bin)
    @objective(bp, Min, sum(y))
    @constraint(bp, capacity[i ∈ M],       # (a)
                V * y[i] >= sum(v[j] * x[i, j] for j ∈ M))
    @constraint(bp, assignment[j ∈ M],     # (b)
                sum(x[i, j] for i ∈ M) == 1)
    optimize!(bp)
    xᵒ, yᵒ = snapvals(value.(x)), snapvals(value.(y))
    used = findall(==(1.0), yᵒ)
    bins = [findall(==(1.0), xᵒ[i, :]) for i ∈ used]
    res = (bins = bins, used = Int(objective_value(bp)),
           status = termination_status(bp), gap = relative_gap(bp),
           secs = solve_time(bp))
    return res
end
```

```text
binpack (generic function with 1 method)
```

```julia

@show packed.bins
@show LB                         # the bound
@show length(trucks)             # first-fit decreasing
packed.used                      # the optimum
```

In Julia, as by hand, first-fit decreasing puts the routes on 4 trucks, and the bin packing model of Lecture 2.7 confirms that 4 is the fewest.

Example 7: Acme’s timed routes to vehicles

Acme, Inc., is a company that supplies 45 customers each day with cases of widgets from its DC in Morrisville, North Carolina, each customer with its own delivery window. Determine its routes within those windows, an hour’s wait at most and a 10-hour route, and the vehicles that can run them, by hand and in Julia.

Acme, Inc., has a DC near the RDU airport in Morrisville, NC that supplies 45 customers each day with identical cases of widgets.

Customer location, demand, and time window data is in the file morrisville-vrptw.csv. The file includes the location of the depot and each customer, number of cases required for each customer, and the time window when the delivery can be made. The time window is indicated by the hours (0 to 24) at which the earliest and latest deliveries can occur. Unloading at each customer must occur within its time window, and the vehicle must wait if it arrives prior to the earliest delivery time. Vehicles can load, depart, and return to the depot at any time.

Each identical vehicle can carry a maximum of 75 cases, must complete its route within 10 total hours, including travel, load/unloading, and waiting time (note: this is a driver-related constraint, thus a vehicle used for multiple routes can be assumed to have a different driver for each route if necessary), must complete its delivery within each customer’s specified time window, and should not wait at a customer for more than one hour, not including unloading time. It takes one hour to load a vehicle at the depot, irrespective of the total number of cases loaded, and two minutes per case at each customer for unloading. Each vehicle travels at an average speed of 35 mph, and road distances are estimated as 1.2 times great circle distances.

Code block 50 reads the customers, their cases and their windows, with each customer’s unloading time at 2 minutes a case, and gives the vehicle its capacity of 75 cases:

```julia
# Code block 50: Morrisville's customers, cases and windows
dm = CSV.read("data/morrisville-vrptw.csv", DataFrame)
XYm = hcat(dm.Longitude, dm.Latitude)         # row 1 is the DC
Tm = 1.2dists(XYm, XYm, :mi) / 35             # h, at 35 mph
nm = nrow(dm)
shm = DataFrame(b = 1, e = 2:nm, q = dm.Cases[2:end],
                tU = 2dm.Cases[2:end] / 60,   # 2 min a case
                temin = dm.Earliest[2:end], temax = dm.Latest[2:end])
trm = (b = 1, e = 1, Kwt = 75)                # 75 cases a vehicle
prt(first(shm, 5))
```

rteTC_vrp reads the capacity and the windows, so Code block 52 first constructs the routes with it alone, and tabulates each route’s time with its hour of loading and its longest wait:

```julia
Rb = [twoopt_rte(r, rTTb)[1] for r in savings(rTTb, shm)]
outb = rteTC_vrp(Rb, shm, Tm, trm)[3]
```

Of its 9 routes, 5 run past 10 hours with the hour of loading, and 4 wait more than an hour somewhere: rteTC_vrp does not have the two limits. Its maximum total cost maxTC cannot stand in for the 10 hours, since it is checked on the travel and unloading before the scans add any waiting, so a route can pass it and still run past 10 hours once its waits and its hour of loading are counted. Code block 53 adds the two limits by a route cost of one’s own, as Sec. 1 adds a maximum distance: it returns infinity for a route that waits more than an hour anywhere, and adds the hour of loading to the route’s time, returning infinity if that is more than 10 hours:

```julia
# Code block 53: the limits rteTC_vrp does not have, a route cost
function rTTm(rte)
    TT, _, out = rteTC_vrp(rte, shm, Tm, trm)
    isinf(TT) && return Inf
    maximum(out.Wait) > 1 && return Inf   # wait at most an hour
    return TT + 1 > 10 ? Inf : TT + 1     # an hour of loading at the DC
end
Rm = [twoopt_rte(r, rTTm)[1] for r in savings(rTTm, shm)]
TTm = rTTm.(Rm)
sum(TTm)
```

```julia
              Back = clock.(em[ks]),
```

11 routes, 80.37 hours with the hour of loading in each, the longest 9.61 hours, every route within 10 hours and no wait over an hour; rteTC_vrp alone gave 9 routes, 5 of them too long.

None of the procedures used so far takes the number of trucks into account. One way to approach it is a Gantt chart, which an industrial engineer has probably seen before, of the beginning and ending times of the routes over the day. From the chart, two routes that do not overlap can be done with one vehicle, two others with a second, one by itself by a third, and perhaps three together by a fourth, going through them systematically by eye. It could be done optimally by finding a directed minimum spanning tree whose forest has as many trees as the minimum number of trucks needed, and with a thousand routes it could not be done by hand; but the directed version is more complicated to implement, and it has not been seen in any package for Julia or Python. Without the optimum, a greedy procedure is easy to code: start with the first route, find one that does not overlap it, combine the two, and go through the routes systematically in that way.

Example 7(b): Routes to vehicles by hand

Determine the vehicles the routes need, by combining routes that do not overlap.

The windows fix when each route runs, so a vehicle can take a second route only if it starts after the first is back. In Code block 54’s table, by the start of loading, the greedy starts with route 9, back at 12:01; the route that starts soonest after that is route 1, loading at 12:40 and back at 19:42, after which no route starts, so vehicle 1 takes routes 9 and 1. Vehicle 2 takes route 6, back at 7:56, and then route 3, loading at 8:36 (route 10 began loading at 7:41, before route 6 was back), and is back at 17:10, after which no route left starts. Vehicle 3 takes route 2, back at 11:40, and every route left starts before then; so does every later route, and routes 4, 10, 11, 5, 8 and 7 each need a vehicle of their own.

Nine vehicles: routes 9 and 1 on one, 6 and 3 on another, and each of the other seven routes on a vehicle of its own.

Example 7(c): In Julia

Determine the fewest vehicles the routes need in Julia, by a model of which route follows which on a vehicle.

The greedy of Ex. 7(b) gives a number of vehicles that is feasible, but not necessarily the fewest. Code block 56 finds the fewest with a model of which route follows which: route $j$ can follow route $i$ on a vehicle only if $j$ starts loading after $i$ is back, and each route has at most one route following it and at most one before it, so each vehicle’s routes form a chain, one tree of the forest in the telling above for each vehicle, and the vehicles are the routes less the links between them:

```julia
# Code block 56: the fewest vehicles, a model of which route follows which
R = 1:length(Rm)
fv = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
set_silent(fv)
@variable(fv, x[i ∈ R, j ∈ R; bm[j] > em[i]], Bin)  # j follows i
@objective(fv, Min, length(R) - sum(x))    # routes less the links
@constraint(fv, next[i ∈ R],               # (a) at most one after i
            sum(x[i, j] for j ∈ R if bm[j] > em[i]) <= 1)
@constraint(fv, before[j ∈ R],             # (b) at most one before j
            sum(x[i, j] for i ∈ R if bm[j] > em[i]) <= 1)
optimize!(fv)
nxt = [findfirst(j -> bm[j] > em[i] && value(x[i, j]) > 0.5, R)
       for i ∈ R]                          # the route after each, if any
veh = Vector{Int}[]
for i ∈ sortperm(bm)                       # by the start of loading
    any(==(i), nxt) && continue            # a route before it
    push!(veh, [i])                        # a vehicle's first route
    while !isnothing(nxt[veh[end][end]])   # and the chain after it
        push!(veh[end], nxt[veh[end][end]])
    end
end
@show veh
Int(objective_value(fv))                   # the fewest vehicles
```

```text
veh = [[9], [6, 8], [2, 1], [4], [10], [3], [11], [5], [7]]
```

The fewest is 9 vehicles, the count of the greedy of Ex. 7(b), with the routes paired differently, since more than one pairing needs that few; Fig. 18 draws each vehicle’s routes against the clock.

If a route could start a little earlier or later, one vehicle might be able to do two routes. Where the windows are tight, that is probably not possible, but in many other cases, when the start is not specified, it is set arbitrarily, since the procedure is concerned only with minimizing the route total cost. If the objective of minimizing the number of vehicles were included instead, the best time to leave could be adjusted: leaving an hour earlier or later might lengthen a route by an hour, which is bad for the route total cost objective, but it might reduce the number of vehicles by one, which is the more important objective. That is not at all included here; it is an extension.

## 4. Tactical routing

The periodic VRP of Sec. 1, which minimizes total logistics cost, is the load formation of Lecture 5.2; tactical routing here is a different question, answered without building any route.

Most routing procedures are for operational decisions, which, given actual demands, determine actual routes; for tactical decisions, a procedure can only estimate routing performance.

Tactical vehicle routing can only estimate routing performance. There is no actual route sequence, but there are overall estimates of how many vehicles would be needed on average over time. It makes extensive use of averaging, pushing the notion as far as it will go, to see what can be said without developing the routes. In many problems, such as how many vehicles to purchase, or at least lease, over the next year to handle the expected routing needs, the actual demands are not known yet; all that is available are estimates of the long-term average future demand. So it makes sense to wring as much useful information out of those estimates as possible, to help determine, for example, how many vehicles to lease, before solving the vehicle routing problem itself.

Tactical routing does not route a set of actual demands, as an operational problem does. It asks, more generally, how much can likely be done in the future given some idea of the demand: not the actual demand, but a forecast or an average. Panel (a) of Fig. 19 is a single distribution center, such as one serving Raleigh, with all of its delivery vans running individual routes, a classic VRP. With such routes it is hard to offer very tight time windows. That is fine when a request is to be delivered sometime during the day, but not for perishable products, which cannot stay on the truck for eight hours and have to be much closer to the customer. The alternative, in panel (b), is many more micro distribution centers, close enough to their customers that no route needs multiple stops: each delivery is point to point, direct to the customer. The analysis behind the figure did not solve any vehicle routing problems to find the average travel times; it used the TSP estimate of Lecture 5.1, which gives enough information, for a given area and number of stops, to estimate the distance that will be traveled. That distance can be translated into travel time, giving the maximum number of stops that can be made within a given time, or the maximum number of customers that can be served in it. That is an application of tactical routing, and its assumption is the estimate’s: customers uniformly distributed in a circle.

Figure 19: Multi-stop deliveries from a single DC (a) against point-to-point deliveries from several DCs (b), for the same set of customers, each DC a yellow square.3

Fig. 19 shows an example of using several multi-stop routes to make deliveries from a single DC versus making point-to-point deliveries from several DCs. In the figure, the total round-trip distance traveled by vehicles for point-to-point deliveries is about twice the distance required to make the same deliveries as part of a multi-stop route, but with point-to-point, after unloading a delivery at home, the vehicle is available to travel back to the DC.

The estimate of Lecture 5.1 applies only to a single tour, or a single route. Most of the time, though, one delivery van cannot deliver to all of the customers in a city such as Raleigh, and several vans are needed. For a parcel carrier, what really limits a van is that there are only eight hours in the day: a van cannot be on the road for 80 hours delivering one day’s packages, and because of that maximum time it takes several vans. In many other delivery problems it is the capacity of the vehicle that limits, not time: a truck delivering appliances may hold only five or six large ones, so five or six is the most stops it can make in an eight-hour day. And in long-distance trucking a route is limited by the 11 hours a driver can spend behind the wheel. So the two constraints seen most are capacity and maximum time. Both can be in effect, but typically one is binding and the other is not.

Lecture 5.1, Sec. 4, estimated the length of a tour from a central DC through $m$ customers spread uniformly over an area $a$ as Eq. 13 in Lecture 5.1:

$$
\hat{d}_m^{TSP} = \varphi\sqrt{ma} \approx 0.908\sqrt{ma}
\tag{8}
$$

where

- $\hat{d}_m^{TSP}$ = estimated length of a tour from a central DC through $m$ customers (mi)
- $m$ = number of customers
- $a$ = area of the region (mi²)
- $\varphi$ = tour constant, fitted to the two-customer route
= $2(\sqrt{2} + 1)/(3\sqrt{\pi}) \approx 0.908$.

Whenever a single tour is broken into several separate routes, there is additional travel to and from the depot termed stem travel. Assuming that the expected one-way stem distance is about the average distance from the center of a circle, the $2r/3$ of Eq. 6 in Lecture 2.5 with $r = \sqrt{a/\pi}$,

$$
\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}}_{\text{1-way}} = \frac{2r}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{a}{\pi}}

$$

Since stem travel occurs both outbound and inbound to the depot, total estimated stem distance is

$$
\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}} = 2\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}}_{\text{1-way}}
= 2\left(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{a}{\pi}}\right)
= \frac{4}{3\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{a} = \kappa\sqrt{a}
\tag{9}
$$

where

- $\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}}_{\text{1-way}}$ = estimated one-way stem distance, depot to first or last stop (mi)
- $\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}}$ = estimated stem distance of a route, out and back (mi)
- $r$ = radius of a circle of area $a$ (mi)
- $\kappa$ = stem constant
= $4/(3\sqrt{\pi}) \approx 0.752$.

For a route to a single customer, the route is all stem, and with $a = \pi r^2$, $\kappa\sqrt{a} = \tfrac{4}{3}r$: the average round trip of the pizza delivery of Ex. 4 in Lecture 1.1, 4 mi for a radius of 3 mi, a Landmark check of Lecture 1.2. Fig. 20 draws a route’s stem and its tour.4,5

Figure 20: A route’s stem (red), out from the depot to its first customer and back from its last, and its tour (blue) through its customers.

Translating the TSP estimate to the VRP adds one complication. A TSP tour leaves the depot, which can be considered one of the customers, visits every customer, and returns to its starting point. With the additional constraints of a VRP, capacity or time, a vehicle has to stop delivering and return to the depot before it has reached all of the customers. The travel beyond what the optimal TSP tour would need, the distance out to a route’s first customer and back from its last, is called the stem distance, and the rest is the tour distance, so a route’s total distance is its stem plus its tour. The name comes from a flower: many vehicle routes look like a rose, the tour being the flower itself and the trip there and back to the depot its stem. To add the stem’s distance, or its time, two thirds of the radius, the average distance from the center of a circle, is used as the one-way stem: not exactly right, but right on average. One way, the stem is $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{a/\pi}$, and there and back it is twice that, $\frac{4}{3\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{a}$. Just as $\varphi$ wraps up the constant of the tour estimate, the Greek letter $\kappa$ wraps up this one, which never changes and is almost exactly 0.75. The Greek letters are kept as a reminder that neither constant is an empirical result. The factors of the LTL rate estimate of Lecture 3.2, Eq. 12 in Lecture 3.2, such as its 7 divided by 2, are just the results of a big regression and have no exact value; under the assumptions here, with two thirds of the radius as the one-way stem, $\kappa$ is an exact value.

In order to be time feasible, vehicle routes must satisfy:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\begin{aligned}
\begin{array}{r}\text{Stem time} + \text{Tour Time} \\ {} + \text{Service Time}\end{array} &\le \text{Vehicle-time capacity} \\
(N - 1)\frac{\hat{d}^{\,\text{stem}}}{v} + \frac{\hat{d}_m^{TSP}}{v} + m t_s &\le N t_{\max} \\
(N - 1)\frac{\kappa\sqrt{a}}{v} + \frac{\varphi\sqrt{ma}}{v} + m t_s &\le N t_{\max}
\end{aligned} \\
\boxed{\;\left[\kappa(N - 1) + \varphi\sqrt{m}\right]\frac{\sqrt{a}}{v} + m t_s \le N t_{\max}\;}
\end{gathered}
\tag{10}
$$

where

- $t_{\max}$ = maximum operating time of a vehicle (h)
- $m$ = number of customers
- $N$ = number of routes, one vehicle each
- $a$ = service area (mi²)
- $t_s$ = service time at each customer (h)
- $v$ = average vehicle speed (mph).

It assumes no capacity constraints, the estimates $\kappa \approx 0.752$ and $\varphi \approx 0.908$ of Eq. 9 and Eq. 8, and that $N - 1$ means no stem travel if there is one vehicle.

Time feasibility is where these results are used, and capacity feasibility follows it. With $N$ routes, one vehicle each, and a maximum operating time $t_{\max}$, the right-hand side of Eq. 10 is the total vehicle hours available: an eight-hour day and ten vehicles give 80 hours, and whatever is done to make all of the deliveries, its total time cannot exceed those 80 vehicle hours. On the left is the total time required. With one vehicle, or one route, it is just a TSP: $N - 1 = 0$ cancels the stem, which is ignored, and what remains is the tour of Lecture 5.1. A distance divided by the travel speed gives a time, since miles over miles per hour leaves hours. Then $m$ is the number of customers and $t_s$ the service time at each, perhaps 2 or 3 minutes for a delivery van: the time it takes a driver to hop out of the van, put the delivery on the porch, take a photo, run back to the van and take off again. All of that added together has to be no more than the vehicle hours available, and with $\kappa$ and $\varphi$ the result is a fairly simple inequality that captures both the stem and the tour, each a multiple of $\sqrt{a}/v$, plus the service time.

Example 8: Delivery estimates

Determine, from the time feasibility of Eq. 10 and without constructing any route, the minimum operating time of three vehicles, the number of deliveries one vehicle can make in eight hours, and the number of deliveries a firm with six trucks has to outsource, by hand and in Julia.

Example 8(a): Minimum operating time

Determine the minimum per-vehicle operating time.

Three vehicles will make deliveries to 100 customers in a 1,000-square-mile service area. Assuming, on average, a vehicle travels at 30 mph (including stops at red lights) and, after reaching a customer, it takes six minutes to drop off a delivery. Estimate the minimum per-vehicle operating time.

In the symbols of Eq. 10, $N = 3$, $m = 100$, $a = 1{,}000$ mi², $v = 30$ mph and $t_s = 6/60$ h, the six minutes in hours, so that every term of the inequality is in hours, a Units check of Lecture 1.2. Dividing Eq. 10 through by $N$ and setting it at equality gives the least $t_{\max}$ the deliveries need:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{\min} &= \frac{\sqrt{a}}{Nv}\left[\kappa(N - 1) + \varphi\sqrt{m}\right] + \frac{m}{N}t_s \\
&= \frac{\sqrt{1000}}{3(30)}\left[0.752(3 - 1) + 0.908\sqrt{100}\right] + \frac{100}{3}\left(\frac{6}{60}\right) \\
&= 0.3514 \times 10.584 + 3.333 = 7.05 \text{ h}
\end{aligned}

$$

With the constants rounded to $\kappa \approx 0.75$ and $\varphi \approx 0.9$, the same working gives 7.02 h; the constants of Eq. 9 and Eq. 8 give 7.05 h.

Three vehicles serving 100 customers need at least 7.05 h each.

The average speed of 30 mph includes the stops at red lights. For a metropolitan area an average of 20 to 25 mph is reasonable, and no more than 35; over a large area such as all of North Carolina, where trucks travel on interstates with few stoplights, an average closer to 65 mph would be used. Over a long trip, a navigation app’s estimate of the arrival time can come out within a couple of minutes, because of the law of large numbers: added up over many small road segments, the over- and underestimates tend to balance out. The minimum operating time is a simple application of a solver: with the givens entered, the time feasibility is forced to be an equality by driving the absolute value of its left-hand side less its right-hand side to zero, and the solver finds the operating time. Here it is simple enough to do algebraically: dividing Eq. 10 through by $N$ gives the service time as $m/N$ times $t_s$ and the travel time as the stem and tour over $N$, and the numbers are put in directly. It is best to get the number numerically first and then make sure it can also be done by hand algebraically; it is always nice to have two different ways. When an algebraic solution gets messy, a numerical solve is the practical choice.

Getting the same number both ways, in Ex. 8(d), is a Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2.

Example 8(b): Deliveries in eight hours

Determine the number of deliveries one vehicle can make in eight hours.

Assuming that, on average, a vehicle travels at 30 mph (including stops at red lights) and, after reaching a customer, it takes two minutes to drop off a delivery. If the service area is fifty square miles, estimate the number of deliveries that the vehicle can make in eight hours assuming that it has no capacity constraints.

With one vehicle, $N = 1$, there is no stem, and Eq. 10 at equality is $m t_s + \varphi\sqrt{ma}/v = t_{\max}$, a quadratic in $\sqrt{m}$ whose root is

$$
m = \frac{a\varphi^2 + 2t_{\max}t_s v^2 - \sqrt{a\varphi^2\left(a\varphi^2 + 4t_{\max}t_s v^2\right)}}{2t_s^2v^2}
\tag{11}
$$

With $a = 50$ mi², $t_s = 2/60$ h, $t_{\max} = 8$ h and $v = 30$ mph,

$$
\begin{aligned}
a\varphi^2 &= 50(0.908)^2 = 41.22 \\
2t_{\max}t_s v^2 &= 2(8)\left(\tfrac{2}{60}\right)30^2 = 480 \\
4t_{\max}t_s v^2 &= 960 \\
2t_s^2v^2 &= 2\left(\tfrac{2}{60}\right)^2 30^2 = 2 \\
m &= \frac{41.22 + 480 - \sqrt{41.22(41.22 + 960)}}{2} \\
&= \frac{521.22 - 203.16}{2} = 159.03
\end{aligned}

$$

Should the estimate be 159 or 160 deliveries? Rounding up to 160 results in total time over 8 h: 159 deliveries take $159 t_s + \varphi\sqrt{159a}/v = 8.00$ h, and 160 take 8.04 h, so the estimate is rounded down, a Bounds check of Lecture 1.2.

One vehicle can make 159 deliveries in eight hours.

With the stops at red lights included, a vehicle that drives at 40 mph or more averages about 30 mph, and 2 minutes to drop off a delivery is about what a parcel delivery takes, 2 to 3 minutes. What is nice is that where the customers are does not have to be known: their number is the unknown, and what is known is the total service area. With the known information put into the time feasibility for a maximum of eight hours, $m$ is the only unknown, and solving for it gives 159. When planning, it gives an idea of how many customers one vehicle can serve. With a holiday season coming next week and an idea of the total demand expected over a metropolitan area, it estimates how many drivers are needed to serve all of it, without seeing the actual demand: an example of what is meant by tactical.

The estimate is an average distance. Roughly speaking, half of the time a route will be longer than the estimate and half of the time shorter. From a design point of view, it may be better to go more to the extremes, wanting to know that, say, 95% of the time the distance will not exceed some value, whereas the average is the middle, the 50% point, of the distribution. That has an impact on how the estimate is applied.

Keeping in mind what the estimate is, an average, is an Assumptions check of Lecture 1.2.

Example 8(c): Outsourcing

Determine the number of deliveries six trucks can make, the number to outsource, and the number of trucks that would need no outsourcing.

Estimated total delivery requirements are 500 for a 200 mi² service area. How many deliveries will have to be outsourced, given the firm has only six trucks? The trucks travel at 25 mph, service time is six minutes, and seven hours are available for delivery.

With $N = 6$, Eq. 10 at equality is again a quadratic in $\sqrt{m}$, now with the stems of five more routes on the right:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_s\left(\sqrt{m}\right)^2 + \frac{\varphi\sqrt{a}}{v}\sqrt{m}
&= N t_{\max} - \frac{\kappa(N - 1)\sqrt{a}}{v} \\
0.1\left(\sqrt{m}\right)^2 + \frac{0.908\sqrt{200}}{25}\sqrt{m}
&= 6(7) - \frac{0.752(5)\sqrt{200}}{25} \\
0.1\left(\sqrt{m}\right)^2 + 0.5136\sqrt{m} - 39.873 &= 0
\end{aligned}

$$

whose positive root gives $m$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{m} &= \frac{-0.5136 + \sqrt{0.5136^2 + 4(0.1)(39.873)}}{2(0.1)} \\
&= \frac{-0.5136 + 4.0265}{0.2} = 17.564 \\
m &= 17.564^2 = 308.51
\end{aligned}

$$

A fractional delivery cannot be made, so $m_{\max} = \lfloor 308.51 \rfloor = 308$, and $500 - 308 = 192$ deliveries have to be outsourced; the rounded constants, 0.75 and 0.9, give 309 and 191. With seven trucks the right-hand side is $7(7) - 0.752(6)\sqrt{200}/25 = 46.448$, so $m = 366.19$ and 134 are outsourced; with eight it is $53.022$, $m = 424.41$, and 76 are. Solving Eq. 10 for $N$ instead, with $m = 500$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
N &\ge \frac{\varphi\sqrt{ma}/v + m t_s - \kappa\sqrt{a}/v}{t_{\max} - \kappa\sqrt{a}/v} \\
&= \frac{0.908\sqrt{500(200)}/25 + 500(0.1) - 0.752\sqrt{200}/25}{7 - 0.752\sqrt{200}/25} \\
&= \frac{11.485 + 50 - 0.425}{7 - 0.425} = \frac{61.060}{6.575} = 9.29
\end{aligned}

$$

so ten trucks would need no outsourcing.

Six trucks can make 308 of the 500 deliveries, so 192 have to be outsourced; seven trucks would outsource 134, eight 76, and ten none.

Ex. 8(c) estimates outsourcing requirements. The firm has only six trucks, and if they cannot make all of the deliveries, the rest have to be served by outsourced trucks. With the number of customers the firm can serve as the unknown, the time feasibility gives 308 whole deliveries, so 192 have to be outsourced. The calculation is useful because outsourcing is probably a lot more expensive per delivery than the firm’s own six trucks and drivers, so it answers what-if questions: buying one or two extra vehicles, seven or eight instead of six, would reduce the outsourcing significantly, at a cost, and whether that is a good deal or a bad one depends on whether 500 a day is the long-run average. A tactical decision of this kind is probably not for multiple years, unless some big contract is being signed, but for the next week or two: an estimate of 500 deliveries a day for a week or two of a Christmas peak, say. The result is then that 192 deliveries a day have to be outsourced for those weeks, and it is probably not worth hiring a permanent employee, since once the season is over the demand drops back, the normal demand being confidently under 300: outsourcing is the choice for the peak period. The same basic tool, time feasibility, answers dozens of mixes and matches of problems like these, but what it leaves off the table is capacity.

Example 8(d): In Julia

Determine the same three estimates in Julia, solving numerically, and how they compare with the hand working.

Code block 58 writes the left-hand side of Eq. 10, the vehicle hours $N$ routes need to serve $m$ customers, as a function:

```julia
# Code block 58: time feasibility, as a function
κ = 4/(3sqrt(π))                         # stem constant, about 0.752
φ = 0.908                                # tour constant, Lecture 5.1
# vehicle hours that N routes need to serve m customers
tfeas(N, m, a, v, ts) = (κ*(N - 1) + φ*sqrt(m))*sqrt(a)/v + m*ts
```

In order to be capacity feasible, a vehicle route must satisfy:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{array}{r}\text{Sum of load size of all} \\ \text{customers along route}\end{array} &\le \text{Vehicle capacity} \\
\frac{m}{N} f &\le q_{\max}
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$

The minimum number of routes and the actual number of routes are

$$
N_{\min} = \left\lceil \frac{mf}{q_{\max}} \right\rceil, \qquad
N = \left\lceil \frac{mf}{q} \right\rceil
\tag{13}
$$

where

- $f$ = customer load size (units)
- $q_{\max}$ = maximum vehicle payload (units)
- $q$ = actual vehicle payload (units)
- $N_{\min}$ = minimum number of routes.

Capacity feasibility is relative to the vehicle’s capacity $q_{\max}$, the combination of cube and weight capacity of trucking in Lecture 3.2, a known piece of data. With $f$ the demand of each customer and $N$ the number of routes, $mf/N$ is how much each vehicle actually serves, and the requirement is that it be no more than the vehicle’s capacity. From it, two things are calculated. One is the minimum number of routes, using the maximum payload. In actuality, though, the primary objective of a vehicle routing problem is usually to reduce the number of vehicles, not to minimize the distance or the travel time, which is secondary: everything else being equal, most companies would rather eliminate one vehicle, even if it increases the distance or travel time a little. So designing just for the maximum payload, though it minimizes the number of routes, may not be the best approach. It can do better to reduce the deliveries, the number of stops, on each route, so that a vehicle is able to make two or even three routes in the time available. With a payload a little less than the maximum in the denominator and the numerator unchanged, the actual number of routes can be greater than the minimum, which Ex. 9 solves by hand.

Example 9: Minimum number of vehicles

Determine the minimum number of vehicles needed for 100 customers of one unit each, when a vehicle carries 5 units, a full route takes 5 hours, 8 hours are available and a vehicle can run more than one route a day, by hand and in Julia.

Example 9(a): Routes per vehicle

Determine the number of vehicles at one, two and three routes per vehicle, and the minimum.

A single delivery route that uses a vehicle’s full capacity of 5 units takes 5 hours to complete. If 8 hours are available, determine the minimum number of vehicles required. There are $m = 100$ customers, each with a load of $f = 1$ unit, and $q_{\max} = 5$ units.

Ex. 9 starts by assuming one route per vehicle. The five hours of a full route would come from the time feasibility of Eq. 10, with the estimates of the tour, the stem travel time and the service time at each customer. With eight hours available, one route per vehicle is feasible, and it takes 20 vehicles for the 20 routes. The procedure, without making it anything too formal, then asks what if each vehicle runs two routes. With eight hours available, each route has four hours, and assuming that the time a route takes is proportional to its load, which from the time feasibility it basically is, four hours over the five of a full route reduces the payload to four units. With four units, 25 routes are needed, and at two routes per vehicle that is 12.5, rounded up to 13 vehicles.

How much time each reduction saves matters. A full route of five units takes five hours, so a route of four units takes four hours and one of three units three hours. With only eight hours available, three three-hour routes cannot fit into eight hours, so three routes per vehicle needs routes of two units. The procedure, done by hand, starts at the maximum payload of five and keeps increasing the number of routes per vehicle, redoing the calculation each time, and keeps whichever result gives the minimum number of vehicles. By the criteria of the VRP, that is the best solution, whatever the distance or the time required: the minimum number of vehicles that can make all of the deliveries within eight hours.

Table 7 takes the steps, a row for each number of routes per vehicle, each payload within Eq. 12 and its routes by Eq. 13:

Table 7: Ex. 9 by routes per vehicle, each route’s payload cut in proportion to its time and, at three routes, to whole units.

| Routes per vehicle | Time per route (h) | Payload (units) | Routes | Vehicles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $t^{(1)} = 5 \le t_{\max}/1 = 8$ | $q = q_{\max} = 5$ | $\lceil 100(1)/5 \rceil = 20$ | $\lceil 20/1 \rceil = 20$ |
| 2 | $t^{(2)} = t_{\max}/2 = 4$ | $q = \frac{t^{(2)}}{t^{(1)}}q_{\max} = \frac{4}{5}(5) = 4$ | $\lceil 100(1)/4 \rceil = 25$ | $\lceil 25/2 \rceil = 13$ |
| 3 | $t^{(3)} = t_{\max}/3 = 2.67$ | $q = \left\lfloor \frac{2.67}{5}(5) \right\rfloor = 2$ | $\lceil 100(1)/2 \rceil = 50$ | $\lceil 50/3 \rceil = 17$ |

Each unit takes $t^{(1)}/q_{\max} = 1$ h of route time, so the 100 units need 100 vehicle hours, and $\lceil 100/8 \rceil = \lceil 12.5 \rceil = 13$ vehicles is a lower bound that two routes per vehicle attains: 13 is the minimum, a Bounds check of Lecture 1.2. The bound is the machine-hours accounting of Lecture 1.3, Sec. 5, with vehicles for machines, the vehicle hours needed over the hours a vehicle has; Eq. 4 in Lecture 1.3 gives $\lfloor 12.5 + 1 \rfloor = 13$ as well, and differs from the ceiling only when the ratio is a whole number, since a workstation’s capacity must strictly exceed its load, while a day’s planned routes can use all of a vehicle’s hours.

At least 13 vehicles are needed, and two routes per vehicle, each carrying 4 units, attains it.

Example 9(b): With loading at the depot

Determine the minimum number of vehicles when each route first takes 20 minutes of loading at the depot.

Ex. 9(a) ignores the reloading time at the DC. With $t_L = 20$ min of loading before each route, as in Ex. 6, a vehicle running two routes has $t^{(2)} = (t_{\max} - 2t_L)/2 = (8 - 2/3)/2 = 3.67$ h for each, a payload of $\lfloor \frac{3.67}{5}(5) \rfloor = 3$ units, $\lceil 100/3 \rceil = 34$ routes and $\lceil 34/2 \rceil = 17$ vehicles; three routes have $t^{(3)} = (8 - 1)/3 = 2.33$ h, 2 units, 50 routes and again 17 vehicles. The loading time erases the four vehicles that two routes saved, a Nudge check of Lecture 1.2: a small change in a given moves the answer a long way, here because whole units cannot shrink by less than one.

With 20 minutes of loading before each route, 17 vehicles are needed, at two or three routes each.

Example 9(c): In Julia

Determine the same steps in Julia, and how they compare with the hand working.

Code block 62 computes a row of Table 7 for each number of routes per vehicle, and the lower bound:

```julia
# Code block 62: Ex. 9, vehicles at one, two and three routes each
m, f, qmax, t1, tmax = 100, 1, 5, 5, 8   # customers, units, units, h, h
rpv = DataFrame(per_vehicle = 1:3)       # routes per vehicle
rpv.t = tmax ./ rpv.per_vehicle          # h for each route
rpv.q = min.(qmax, floor.(Int, rpv.t ./ t1 .* qmax))   # whole units
rpv.N = ceil.(Int, m*f ./ rpv.q)         # routes
rpv.vehicles = ceil.(Int, rpv.N ./ rpv.per_vehicle)
prt(rpv)
@show ceil(Int, m*f*(t1/qmax)/tmax);     # the time bound
```

```text
─────────────────────────────────────
1            1  8.00  5  20        20
2            2  4.00  4  25        13
3            3  2.67  2  50        17
ceil(Int, (m * f * (t1 / qmax)) / tmax) = 13
```

Tactical routing is much of what an industrial engineer actually does with vehicle routing. Operational routing has become a commodity, in that very good software for it is easy to find. But the operational problem gives no long-term insight into questions such as how many vehicles to lease for a peak period, and those are tactical decisions. Little software does the tactical part; its logic tends to be embedded in an expensive transportation management system, which brings the whole baggage of a commercial software package with it, and it is better to isolate the tactical decision making itself. It boils down to simple calculations like those of Ex. 8 and 9, all predicated on the TSP estimate, so whatever validity its assumptions have carries over. In practice it works pretty well: a mathematician might frown on it, but for engineering purposes it is a pretty effective approach. The questions companies typically have are of this kind: they are not so much interested in what the routes would be as in answers that operational routing cannot give, and tactical routing is a way of looking at such problems and coming up with actual recommendations.

Example 10: North Carolina counties on road time

Determine how many routes a DC at the center of North Carolina needs to deliver to each of the other 99 counties on road time, under the hours of service of Lecture 3.2, first by estimate and then by savings, and how the two compare.

The counties of Lecture 5.1, drawn with their shortest tour on the roads in Fig. 15 in Lecture 5.1, are the customers, one delivery each, 30 minutes at each, and the times between them are the fastest road times of Lecture 4.1, Sec. 5.6 Code block 64 builds the road network around the county points as Ex. 4 in Lecture 5.1 did, times each link as Ex. 3 in Lecture 4.1 did, and keeps the hours between every pair of counties:

```julia
# Code block 64: the counties, and the road time between every pair
using SimpleWeightedGraphs
dfc = filter(r -> (r.STFIP == st2fips(:NC)), uscounty())
a = sum(dfc.ALAND) + sum(dfc.AWATER)             # mi²
Nf, Lf = prune_reindex(faf5nodes(), faf5links()) # Lecture 4.1's network
Nc, Lc = cropnetwork(Nf, Lf, dfc.LON, dfc.LAT)   # a box around the points
Nc, Lc = addconnectors(Nc, Lc, dfc.LON, dfc.LAT; add_nf_nf = false)
con = isequal.(Lc.SOURCE, "CONNECTOR")
# A link's minutes: FAF5's free-flow time t, or, where a link has none,
# 60 d / v at its posted speed v; a connector at 20 mph
mins(t, v, d) = t > 0 ? t : 60d / v
tAB = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)
       for (c, t, v, d) in zip(con, Lc.AB_TIME, Lc.SPEED, Lc.DIST)]
tBA = [c ? 60d / 20 : mins(t, v, d)
       for (c, t, v, d) in zip(con, Lc.BA_TIME, Lc.SPEED, Lc.DIST)]
fw, bw = Lc.DIR .!= -1, Lc.DIR .!= 1             # each link's directions
gT = SimpleWeightedDiGraph([Lc.SRC[fw]; Lc.DST[bw]],
                           [Lc.DST[fw]; Lc.SRC[bw]],
                           [tAB[fw]; tBA[bw]]; combine = min)
Tmin, PT = shortestpaths(gT, nrow(dfc))          # minutes, and the paths
Tc = Tmin / 60                                   # h
@show maximum(Tc);                               # the longest drive, h
```

```text
maximum(Tc) = 9.572079284922552
```

Code block 65 puts the DC at the county nearest the center of the state, each county weighted by its area:

```julia
# Code block 65: the DC, at the county nearest the center of the state
wc = dfc.ALAND + dfc.AWATER                      # each county's area
ctr = [sum(wc .* dfc.LON), sum(wc .* dfc.LAT)] / sum(wc)   # weighted
dc = argmin([dgc(ctr, [dfc.LON[i], dfc.LAT[i]]) for i in 1:nrow(dfc)])
dfc.NAME[dc]
```


The estimate of Eq. 8 measures distance in a straight line across the state, so its speed has to be fitted to the roads: the speed at which the estimated length of a tour of all 100 counties is covered in the time of the fastest tour on the roads, found by the TSP formulation of Lecture 5.1 (Code block 9):

```julia
# Code block 66: the fastest tour of the counties, and its speed
ncT = TSP(Tc)                                    # Lecture 5.1, road hours
@show ncT.TC                                     # h
@show v = φ * sqrt(nrow(dfc) * a) / ncT.TC;      # mph, over the area
```

```text
ncT.TC = 71.89435778127594
v = (φ * sqrt(nrow(dfc) * a)) / ncT.TC = 29.299288394453633
```

Before any route is built, Eq. 10 solved for $N$, as in Ex. 8(c), gives the number of routes each limit of the hours of service needs: 11 h of driving, without the service time, and 14 h on duty, with it. Committing to that count first is a Prior check of Lecture 1.2:

```julia
# Code block 67: the routes the estimate needs, before any is built
m, ts = nrow(dfc) - 1, 30 / 60                   # customers, h at each
stem = κ * sqrt(a) / v                           # h out and back
tour = φ * sqrt(m * a) / v                       # h, all m customers
@show (tour - stem) / (11 - stem)                # routes: 11 h driving
@show (tour + m * ts - stem) / (14 - stem);      # routes: 14 h on duty
```

```text
(tour - stem) / (11 - stem) = 13.001775829907281
((tour + m * ts) - stem) / (14 - stem) = 14.306474470389658
```

The time on duty binds, and the estimate is 15 routes. Code block 68 then builds the routes by savings, each county a delivery from the DC, with the hours-of-service route cost of Ex. 5(b) written for this example’s shipments, times and truck:

```julia
# Code block 68: routes by savings, under the hours of service
shc = DataFrame(b = dc, e = setdiff(1:nrow(dfc), dc))  # a delivery each
shc.tU .= ts                                     # h unloading at each
trc = (b = dc, e = dc)                           # from the DC and back
function rTTc(rte)                 # hours of service, as Ex. 5(b)
    TT, _, out = rteTC_vrp(rte, shc, Tc, trc)
    isinf(TT) && return Inf
    drive = sum(out.Cost)          # time at the wheel
    return drive > 11 || TT > 14 ? Inf : TT   # 11 h in a 14 h day
end
Rc = savings(rTTc, shc)
@show length(Rc)
@show count(isinf, rTTc.(Rc));                   # routes it cannot run
```

```text
length(Rc) = 17
count(isinf, rTTc.(Rc)) = 3
```

3 of the 17 routes cost infinity: each is a single county that cannot be served within the hours of service even alone, and savings returns them without saying so. Code block 69 names them, sets them aside, and improves the other routes by 2-opt:

```julia
# Code block 69: the counties set aside, and the routes improved
gone = [rte2idx(r)[1] for r in Rc if isinf(rTTc(r))]   # infeasible alone
println(dfc.NAME[shc.e[gone]])
Rc = [twoopt_rte(r, rTTc)[1] for r in Rc if isfinite(rTTc(r))]
drive = [sum(rteTC_vrp(r, shc, Tc, trc)[3].Cost) for r in Rc]
prt(DataFrame(stops = length.(rte2idx.(Rc)), drive = drive,
              duty = rTTc.(Rc)))
@show length(Rc)
@show sum(rTTc.(Rc));                            # h on duty
```

Cherokee, Clay and Graham, in the far west, are more than 11 hours of driving out and back from Lee County with their 30 minutes, an Assumptions check of Lecture 1.2: a central DC cannot serve the whole state under the hours of service, and the estimate, which assumes it can, has to be redone for the 96 counties served:

```julia
# Code block 70: the estimate for the counties served
ms = m - length(gone)                            # customers served
@show (φ * sqrt(ms * a) / v + ms * ts - stem) / (14 - stem);
```

For the counties served the estimate is 13.98, so 14 routes, the 14 savings built, a Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2. Fig. 21 draws them.

Figure 21: The 14 routes from Lee County under the hours of service, each in its own color and numbered near the center of its counties, each leg along its fastest roads in the FAF5 network of 2022, the county points in ink, the three counties set aside marked ×, and the routes’ hours on duty at the lower right.

The estimate of 15 routes, made before any route was built, assumed every county could be served; 3 in the far west cannot, and for the other 96 the estimate, 14 routes, is what savings builds.

The stem in the literature. Daganzo and Hall, whose paper is the next endnote, estimate the distance of a set of vehicle routes from a depot in the same two parts, for $C$ deliveries per vehicle and points of density $\delta$, as $d \approx 2\bar{r}/C + k/\sqrt{\delta}$ per point. Here $\bar{r}$ is the average distance from a stop to the depot, and $k$ is a dimensionless constant that depends on the metric, about 0.57 for Euclidean distance and 0.82 for rectilinear. The first term, the line-haul term, summed over all of the points, is the distance vehicles would travel if their only task were to reach the center of a district and return to the depot.

Summed over $m$ points on $N = m/C$ routes, with $\delta = m/a$, it is $2\bar{r}N + k\sqrt{ma}$. With the depot at the center of a circle, $2\bar{r} = \kappa\sqrt{a}$ of Eq. 9, so their line-haul term is the stem of every route; Eq. 10 counts $N - 1$ stems instead, because the tour of Eq. 8 already passes through the DC once, and its tour constant $\varphi$ covers the whole tour where their $k$ covers only the local travel, so the two constants are not interchangeable. Lecture 5.1’s dropdown “The constant in the literature” sets $\varphi$ beside Christofides and Eilon’s constant for the whole tour.

-

C. F. Daganzo and R. W. Hall, “A Routing Model for Pickups and Deliveries: No Capacity Restrictions on the Secondary Items,” Transportation Science 27(4), 1993, 315–329; Eq. 2 and its terms on p. 317.

-

Shortest against fastest roads. Taking each leg by its fastest route is not the same as taking the shortest. On the same roads, the shortest tour of the counties by distance shares 71 of its 100 legs with the fastest tour of Code block 66, but only 14 in the same direction: the two run mostly in opposite directions around much the same circuit. Driving the shortest tour, each leg by its shortest route, takes 12.3% more time than the fastest tour, the difference between the shortest and the fastest route of Lecture 4.1 at the scale of a whole tour.
